Source: BBC News Score: 2.54
- Published Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs. This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon. Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity. They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything". Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post. "We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X. While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm. Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products. Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species". One conference speaker, Grindr chief executive George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic". He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology. "It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said. "Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'" Anthropic was valued at $965bn (£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year. The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements. In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious". Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments before a crowd at the conference, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue. Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense". And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers. Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a duopoly in the sector. Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole". On Friday, chief executive of AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety. "Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective." Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety. Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei. Could insider warnings prompt a crackdown? In April, Anthropic roiled the AI world when it said it found that its Mythos tool could outperform humans at some hacking and cybersecurity tasks. Mythos also showed the ability to independently escape what is known as the sandbox environment, setting off a debate among regulators, legislators and businesses about AI's potential dangers. In a new development on Thursday, Anthropic said it had found and stopped threat actors who were trying to use its AI technology for activity including the development of bioweapons and cyber-espionage. Beneath the sparkling chandeliers hanging in the stained-glass dome atrium of The Palace Hotel, some investors told the BBC that the comments from Coxon and others could accelerate a government crackdown. Federal legislation co-sponsored this month by left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, known as the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, would impose a temporary pause in advanced AI development. "There is a good chance that human beings will lose control over AI," Sanders told the BBC's Newsnight programme on Thursday. "And what happens then, nobody knows. But could it be catastrophic? Yes, it could." "When scientists tell you there is a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he added. If an industry-wide government crackdown comes, however, it is likely to be led by legislators and not the Trump administration which largely supports a policy of unfettered AI development. It has framed this as necessary to ensure the US does not cede dominance to China. Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now." But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal. David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic. OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership". The company did not respond to a BBC inquiry seeking comment. At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI. OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn, has previously announced plans to allow people to buy shares in its firm by listing on the stock market. However, its chief executive Sam Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year, calling it an "ill-advised moment" to do so "given everything happening with safety" in an interview with Fortune magazine. He suggested 2027 would be more likely. Meanwhile, one investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares. His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable? When asked on Thursday if he fears the world may be coming to an end, Sid Sheth - chief executive of the chip company d-Matrix which inked a deal with Nvidia at the conference that day - did not mince his words. "No," he said.

item.title: Russia hits Ukrainian train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.20
- Published A Russian drone has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through. No casualties were reported after the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. All the passengers had been evacuated, Ukrainian authorities said. Johnson and other European national security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on a different train on their way back from a conference in Kyiv. Russia said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said that "quite possibly, the target of this drone could have been the diplomatic train". Former CIA chief David Petraeus, who had been on board another train at Yahodyn station at the time of the strike, said the incident was "terrifying". In an interview with the New York Times, Petraeus said: "This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorize Ukrainian civilians." In a statement, Ukrzaliznytsia said the train "had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes". It also said an evacuation order for passengers on the hit train had been given "just 15 minutes" before the strike by a Russian jet-propelled drone. Both Ukrainian and Polish authorities said the Russian drone had struck 2km from the Polish border. Former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, who had also attended the conference in Kyiv, told the BBC passengers on board his train had been told to prepare for evacuation before subsequently being allowed to continue their journey. "On the train I was on we received order to prepare evacuation after it had stopped. But after a number of minutes we were informed that it was clear and we could proceed," he said. That train then safely arrived at Poland's border station in Dorohusk. Some reports have suggested Bildt was on the same train as Johnson, but the former UK prime minister has not confirmed any details. Johnson wrote on X: "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning. He said this was "the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day - even on civilian railways" and urged Kyiv's allies to urgently provide Ukrainians "the air defences they need". Ukraine has made repeated pleas to its allies - particularly the US - to provide more interceptors to defend against daily Russian attacks that increasingly use fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-propelled drones. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric strikes" at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn amounted to "[Russian President Vladimir] Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and Nato" and renewed calls for more sanctions on Moscow. "Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level. This is the only way to stop him," he said. In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk held an emergency meeting to discuss the latest developments. "The escalation of the actions from the Russian side is becoming a reality, and they are getting closer and closer to our border." Johnson and other top European security advisers were on their way back from the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv - an annual event that brings together leaders and experts from politics, business, security and mass media. Russia appears to be escalating its war against Ukraine by targeting trains, railway depots, petrol stations and border crossings. Earlier this week, two people were killed when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Also this week, a female conductor died in a Russian drone attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine. Six Ukrzaliznytsia employees were killed after a depot was struck n Kyiv at the start of the month. In January, Zelensky condemned as "terrorism" a Russian strike on a crowded passenger train in the north-eastern Kharkiv region that left five people dead. The Russian attacks have significantly damaged Ukraine's vast train network - the main mode of transportation for millions of Ukrainians as all air travel has been suspended since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. European countries are also blaming Russia for suspicious incidents on their territory. Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd". There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.

item.title: A 43-year-old with colon cancer used AI in 3 ways to help make treatment a little easier
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.71
Russ Read-Barrow has been living with incurable stage four colon cancer for five years. The 43-year-old former PR director and father of two from the UK was diagnosed with the disease in 2021. After seeing blood in his poop around six times over the course of a few weeks, he got a colonoscopy. With multiple rounds of chemotherapy and surgeries to remove cancerous cells from his colon, liver, and later his lungs, Read-Barrow's doctors have stopped the cancer from spreading further since 2022. He still needs regular chemotherapy, roughly every three months, to slow cell division and prevent further growth in his lungs and liver. "The chemo I'm having now is doing a good job of keeping it under control, but at some point that'll change and I'll have to have something else," Read-Barrow told Business Insider. Over the years, Read-Barrow has experimented with using AI to help manage the symptoms, medications, and emotional challenges that have become part of his life. In 2025, he launched a side project called FcancerwithAI, a blog where he shares his story and the AI cancer tools he's built. "I'm not saying AI is going to cure cancer. I'm saying it's going to help me remember what my consultant said, spot patterns in my side effects, and maybe give me back some control in a situation where control is basically an illusion," he wrote in a blog post. He hopes that by sharing what has helped him, he can help others, as rates of colon cancer cases in those under 50 have risen since the mid-1990s, making it the deadliest cancer in this age group. However, if spotted early, the survival rate for colon cancer is high, meaning, like Read-Barrow, more and more people are living with cancer as a chronic illness. Here are three ways Read-Barrow has used AI to manage his ongoing cancer treatment. Chemotherapy symptom tracker Russ-Barrow will need chemo for the foreseeable future. Afterwards, he typically experiences side effects like fatigue, nausea, and changes to his mood and sleep habits, which can be hard to cope with. "The hardest part day-to-day is trying to manage the energy windows I do have," he said. He started recording a 30-second voice note chronicling his symptoms each day following chemo, and wearing a WHOOP health tracker. He did this for three cycles of chemo and plugged his information into Claude to spot patterns in how he felt and what exacerbated or eased symptoms. "I found it really useful," he said. The data showed that by around day four after his treatment, he would go from feeling relatively normal to exhausted. "If you see that over time happening again and again, you can sort of deal with it better because you know it's going to come and you don't think, 'Oh God, what's happening?'" he said. Subsequently, he started asking the AI to pick out 10 things he should remember before starting his next round of chemo. One of the things it reminded him was that an anti-nausea medication he tried had helped. "You don't keep a record, you won't remember. You think you will, but give it three months and life will take over and you won't," he said. A medical history research assistant Read-Barrow uploaded all of his medical records to Gemini Notebook (formerly Notebook LM). The AI is designed to answer questions, spot trends, and create content such as presentation decks based only on files the user uploads. He uses it as a "centralized hub" for all of his medical records, which means he can access test results, doctor's notes or any other medical data within seconds. "It saves me from the massive admin headache of digging through folders every time I see a specialist," he said. Getting new people up to speed When signing up for a gym, getting a treatment such as a massage, or seeing any kind of doctor, they typically ask for your medical history. However, when you have a complex chronic illness like cancer, that history can be lengthy and painful to recount. He found a solution by asking Gemini Notebook to summarize his health history in 500 words, which he can pass on. Read-Barrow is aware that not everyone would feel comfortable sharing so much personal information with AI platforms, but for him, the benefits outweigh the risks. "I've got terminal cancer. What's the worst that can bloody happen?" he said. This article is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always consult your qualified physician or healthcare provider.

item.title: The 19 actors with the most Emmy wins of all time
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.47
An Emmy is the biggest award an actor can win for their work on the small screen — and when there's a show or a performance Emmy voters love, it often gets multiple nominations and wins. We've pored over the stats and compiled a list of the most Emmy-awarded actors of all time. It includes some of the biggest TV stars of all time, including Bryan Cranston, Betty White, Mary Tyler Moore, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. In fact, Louis-Dreyfus is tied with Cloris Leachman for eight Emmy wins as a performer and with Carl Reiner for the most total Emmy wins among the actors on this list, with 11, if you include their awards in other categories, too. The total Emmy wins listed here aren't exclusively for performances: Some on this list have won for writing, directing, or producing — Cranston was a producer on "Breaking Bad," and Louis-Dreyfus is an executive producer for "Veep," for example — but the majority of their Emmys are for acting. Here are the actors with the most Emmy wins. Carrie Wittmer contributed to a prior version of this article. 15 (tie). Don Knotts — 5 wins and 5 nominations Knotts was nominated for five Emmy Awards (in 1961, 1962, 1963, 1966, and 1967) for his performance as Barney Fife in "The Andy Griffith Show" — and he won them all. 15 (tie). John Larroquette — 5 wins and 7 nominations Larroquette won four consecutive Emmys from 1985 to 1988 for his performance in "Night Court." His last win came for his guest role in "The Practice" in 1998. 15 (tie). Candice Bergen — 5 wins and 9 nominations All five of Bergen's wins came from her performance as the titular role in the CBS sitcom "Murphy Brown." She was nominated for an additional two awards in the 2000s for "Boston Legal." 15 (tie). Peter Falk — 5 wins and 12 nominations All but one of Falk's Emmys came from his long-running performance as one of the most iconic TV detectives: Frank Columbo on "Columbo." He also won in 1962 for "The Dick Powell Show." 11 (tie). Tim Conway — 6 wins and 13 nominations Conway was nominated for both his acting and his writing. He won for acting on "The Carol Burnett Show," "Coach," and "30 Rock." 11 (tie). Michael J. Fox — 5 wins and 19 nominations Fox won three consecutive Emmys in '86, '87, and '88 for playing Alex P. Keaton in "Family Ties." He won another two for "Spin City" and "Rescue Me." In 2026, he was nominated for his guest appearance on "Shrinking," but lost to Rob Reiner, who won posthumously for his appearance on "The Bear." 11 (tie). Kelsey Grammer — 5 wins and 17 nominations Four of Grammer's wins came from his long-running performance as Frasier Crane on "Frasier." His fifth (and most recent) win came from his vocal performance as Sideshow Bob in an episode of "The Simpsons." 11 (tie). Betty White — 5 wins and 21 nominations White's wins were for "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," "The Golden Girls," "The John Larroquette Show," and "Saturday Night Live." 8 (tie). Art Carney — 6 wins and 12 nominations Carney won four times for "The Jackie Gleason Show," once for "The Honeymooners," and once for the made-for-TV film "Terrible Joe Moran." 8 (tie). Tyne Daly — 6 wins and 16 nominations In 1983, 1984, 1985, and 1988, Daly took home the Emmy Award for lead actress in a drama series for "Cagney and Lacey." She won twice more in 1996 and 2003 for roles in "Christy" and "Judging Amy," respectively. 8 (tie). Alan Alda — 6 wins and 34 nominations Alda won five Emmys across acting, writing, and directing on "MASH." His last win came in 2006 for appearing on "The West Wing." 4 (tie). Bryan Cranston — 7 wins and 16 nominations 4 (tie). Allison Janney — 7 wins and 15 nominations 4 (tie). Ed Asner — 7 wins and 17 nominations Asner won for "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," "Rich Man, Poor Man," "Roots," and "Lou Grant." Asner's wins for "The Mary Tyler Moore Show" and "Lou Grant" made him one of the few actors to win for playing the same character across two different shows. 4 (tie). Mary Tyler Moore — 7 wins and 15 nominations Moore won twice for "The Dick Van Dyke Show," four times for "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," and once for the TV movie "Stolen Babies." 3. Cloris Leachman — 8 wins and 22 nominations If we're just counting performances, Leachman would be tied for No. 2; however, the two actors above her have also won for writing and producing. Leachman won for acting in "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," "A Brand New Life," "Cher," the "Screen Actors Guild 50th Anniversary Celebration," "Promised Land," and "Malcolm in the Middle" across 33 years. 1 (tie). Carl Reiner — 11 wins and 18 nominations Reiner's three acting Emmys came from "Caesar's Hour" and "Mad About You." His other eight wins came from writing and producing "The Dick Van Dyke Show" and "The Sid Caesar, Imogene Coca, Carl Reiner, Howard Morris Special." 1 (tie). Julia Louis-Dreyfus — 11 wins and 26 nominations Most famously, Louis-Dreyfus won a record-breaking six consecutive Emmy Awards for playing Selina Meyer on "Veep" (she also won three more for producing the show). She won one Emmy apiece for her performances on "Seinfeld" and "The New Adventures of Old Christine," as well.

item.title: Anthropic has chosen the Nasdaq for its IPO listing
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.46
Anthropic has selected the Nasdaq for its potential IPO, according to a person familiar with their plans. The company, which has been targeting an October listing, has given Nasdaq another big win, according to a person familiar with the matter. Nasdaq secured the coveted SpaceX listing earlier this year. SpaceX was valued at $1.75 trillion, and some estimates have put Anthropic at $2 trillion, though that figure has not yet been finalized. The record-setting size of these IPOs, combined with the dearth in tech listings in recent years, has made winning this competition particularly valuable. Both hope to be seen as the home for future AI IPOs. Anthropic is preparing to IPO at a time when OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says that it wouldn't go public right now amid the controversy surrounding existential threats from AI. That risk gained more attention last week after a viral tweet from a former Anthropic employee, warning of a greater than 10% human extinction risk. Historically, the New York Stock Exchange has won many of the largest listings, but Nasdaq has remained strong in tech, with large listings including Cerebras and Rivian. Listings on its exchange a prerequisite for inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 Index. In terms of how Anthropic ultimately trades, this decision likely matters little. There isn't a definitive answer on whether companies perform better on one exchange versus another. One key difference between the exchanges concerns market-maker mechanics. They have different processes for determining the opening price on the first day of trading, and high-volume IPOs can cause delays and confusion. Nasdaq experienced technical issues on the first day of Facebook's 2012 IPO. Anthropic's IPO filing has not yet been made public, but the company will need to release its financials at least 15 days before it begins its investor road show. Have a tip? Contact Katie Roof via email at kroof@businessinsider.com or Signal at @kroof.26

item.title: Dario Amodei says OpenAI's Hugging Face hack helped convince him AI needs to slow down
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.42
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's "become convinced" in recent months that AI needs to slow down. And rogue OpenAI agents are part of the reason. Amodei cited the July Hugging Face breach, in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing environment to hack into the AI platform and then hide their tracks, as one of the catalysts for his heightened alarm. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet," he wrote in a blog post published Saturday. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Saturday that he agreed with Amodei. "We need to pace the frontier," he said on X. "This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks." Elon Musk, whose SpaceXAI competes with Anthropic and OpenAI, also backed Amodei's proposition on Saturday, writing in an X post, "Dario is right." Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google's AI program, DeepMind, said on X that "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward." He reminded everyone that two months ago, he outlined his own vision for how AI should be developed and governed. Amodei also cited the rapid advancement of AI in recent months and its increased capacity for "recursive self-improvement," which is essentially an AI model's ability to learn on its own. Amodei proposed a three-step plan to slow down AI development to ensure the tech's safety "while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas." Central to Amodei's plan is embedding independent safety evaluators inside frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, giving them "employee-like access" to the companies' systems and work. "This is the key step for verifiability of any pacing commitments," Amodei wrote. "Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now." In his X post, Altman said OpenAI would also implement third-party evaluators into its company. "We'll have more to share soon," he said. The AI community has been in a furor this week after Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon quit, issuing a public warning that AI agents could "kill us all by the end of the decade." Coxon's warnings were shared widely and signal-boosted by other Anthropic employees, one of whom, the company's alignment science lead, said on X, "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" On Saturday, Coxon reposted Musk's "Dario is right" post. Earlier in the week, Musk accused Coxon of orchestrating a "setup." OpenAI's chief scientist, meanwhile, also said in a blog post last week that leading AI labs need to coordinate a slowdown. "No one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Jakub Pachocki said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman reposted Pachocki's comments on X, calling it an "important post." Bloomberg reported this week that, during an employee meeting, Altman said OpenAI was willing to slow AI development in conjunction with rival labs. In his Saturday essay, Amodei reiterated previous calls for the US government to intervene and establish guidelines for American labs. The Trump administration, so far, has resisted regulating the American AI industry to maintain its narrowing lead over Chinese AI labs. Democratic lawmakers, for their part, proposed stringent legislation this week that would severely hamper AI development. Sen. Bernie Sanders, in a recent interview with MSNOW, said AI companies "need to stop right now." Amodei and other leading AI researchers and engineers have not argued for a full stop to development. In his essay, Amodei said American AI labs should continue developing, just with more robust safeguards. He said there remains a need to compete with China, and said the Trump administration could ensure this by not selling the rival the advanced chips needed to power AI models. "The stakes are too high for pacing to be an empty exercise — we need to use the time it gives us wisely," Amodei said.

item.title: The US military is preparing for mass casualties in a major war. Its dentists say it's overlooking toothaches.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.65
A painful toothache or an oral infection might not sound like an injury that could sideline a soldier in combat, but US Army dental leaders warn that in a future conflict, such easily overlooked conditions could take troops out of the fight, consume scarce evacuation capacity, and further stress a strained medical system. Most of the Army's major exercises don't include dental emergencies in their casualty scenarios, dentists said in a recent professional article, leaving commanders with an incomplete picture of the medical and triage or evacuation demands they could face in large-scale combat. Dental emergencies can quickly render troops "non-mission-capable," the authors wrote, because pain can make it difficult to eat, think clearly, or carry out important tasks like operating weapons. They described this as a significant "hidden casualty load." Unlike combat wounds, most dental problems can be easily fixed if dental teams are nearby, but despite their important role in military health care, "deployable dental capabilities continue to decline," authors wrote, underscoring an "urgent need for accurate dental emergency modeling in war-gaming to emphasize the importance of [non-battle related injuries] and dental emergencies." Past wars indicate substantial demand. Dental emergencies accounted for 19% of all treatment at military hospitals near the front lines during the war in Iraq. Another recent article by Army dentists said that dental disease and other non-battle injuries made up nearly 16% of all medical evacuations among troops fighting the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. Almost all dental patients treated by forward dental teams returned to duty after one or two visits, the authors wrote. Without dental care close to the front, however, soldiers may have to travel farther to receive treatment, potentially removing them from duty for as long as a week. Casualty evacuations for any type of health concern or injury, major or minor, are likely to pose a problem for the military in future large-scale combat. The proliferation of drones, both attack and surveillance systems, across the Ukrainian battlefield have made quick evacuation largely impossible, a stark difference from the US experience during the post-9/11 wars. In a recent military news release for a healthcare training event, Army dentist Lt. Col. Jesse Thietten said dental care "is a low-hanging-fruit solution for medical as a whole. Military medicine needs solutions to account for the anticipated systemic medical overload in [large-scale conflicts.]" Dental emergencies could rank among the top five most common reasons for casualty evacuation in such a fight, Thietten added. For troops deployed abroad in multinational settings alongside partner forces, dental concerns are "the number one reason" for casualty evacuation, he added. Thietten helped develop a lightweight expeditionary dental platform for special operations teams training in remote parts of Europe, where teams asked for help treating dental emergencies without easy access to traditionally robust medical facilities. The goal was to bring care closer to troops rather than having to shuttle them to far-off clinics. Such an approach reflects what Thietten argues the broader force will need in a future fight, including more dental work before troops deploy, along with smaller, more mobile dental teams that can operate close to units in the field. Within the Air Force, less than 1% of the service's dentists deploy," said Air Force Col. Anita Shade, chief of dental services for the 21st Medical Group, in the same news release. "Our dental teams are often disconnected from the heart of the readiness mission that we work to support, day in and day out," she said. That disconnect may become more pronounced when combat casualties can't easily be moved from the battlefield to established hospitals and care facilities. "Asymmetric/hybrid drone warfare shows us that we now need to plan and prepare for prolonged patient management in the field due to the unpredictability of patient transport," Shade said. Another problem for some military dentists is more basic — broken field equipment and a lack of medical supplies, hampering training opportunities. Two Army dentists cited those problems in another article from this summer on how military dentistry must adapt for future conflict. While preparing for a unit exercise, they found that their field equipment had not been used in nearly a year and that critical equipment including their sterilizer unit was broken, underscoring further readiness challenges.

item.title: My partner and I split our lives between the US and Canada — and have no plans to pick just one place
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.46
For a week every month, I take a two-and-a-half-hour flight from Chicago to Winnipeg, Canada. That might sound surprising: It's a lot of time to spend in the air, and Chicago has so much to offer. However, I've been in a long-distance relationship with my Canadian partner, Andrew, for over two years, and neither of us is ready to move just yet. Andrew and I met at a conference for financial bloggers a decade ago, and we were great friends and colleagues for many years before we became a couple. Today, we run an online business together, which allows us to work remotely and travel regularly between our countries. Because we both have children from previous marriages, neither of us plans to move countries anytime soon. There are challenges, but I feel like I get the best of both worlds As an American, I've gotten used to certain apps, tools, and conveniences that I can't access in Canada. For example, Canada doesn't have Venmo or Cash App, so Andrew and I split costs or pay each other back using Wise. If we start a movie on Hulu, we can only watch it when we're in the States, since the streaming service isn't available in Canada. As inconvenient as that can be, I often feel like I get the best of both worlds. Take food, for instance: Andrew looks forward to getting Chick-fil-A when he visits me, because there isn't a location in Winnipeg. (Although the chain does exist in some bigger Canadian cities, like Toronto.) And, though we have A&W here in the US, it doesn't have poutine on the menu, which is the unofficial Canadian national dish. So, I always make sure to order that when I visit him. I've found that the pace and culture feel very different in both places, too. As someone who's been self-employed for almost 15 years, I appreciate being able to surround myself with other motivated entrepreneurs whenever I'm here. In Winnipeg and other Canadian cities I've visited, though, I've been able to slow down more. The pace feels more relaxed, and I often think of Canada as my safe haven. In the future, we might choose both There are also structural differences between the two places. Canadians fund their universal healthcare system through taxes, whereas a majority of Americans have private insurance. What's nice about Canada's system is that residents don't have to stress about an unexpected bill or an expensive ER visit. That said, there can be trade-offs, like longer wait times for emergency care and surgeries. In the US, I appreciate that I can usually make medical appointments quickly, even though they come at a cost. There are parts of American culture that will always feel hard to leave, but spending so much time in Canada has also shown me that stepping away from hustle culture can be soothing for my soul. There are parts of American life that Andrew appreciates, too — but I know that if we live elsewhere, he'll miss many aspects of his home, like his close-knit family and the beautiful, wide-open prairies in Winnipeg. I'm not sure what the future holds once all our kids go to college, but we will likely spend half the year in Canada and then work remotely in a warmer area during the winter. Whatever we choose, I know what will matter most is making sure we create a lifestyle that feels unique to us, a perfect blend of our cultures together.

item.title: Grandma's 72 and still working to support her children — and theirs
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.34
Joann Ernst, 72, shook her head as her older grandson decapitated an action figure. The other laid out puzzle pieces in a line, surrounded by a sea of toys. "You have to put all the Play-Doh back in the container so it doesn't dry out," Ernst called out to the 5- and 7-year olds. Ernst is not the boys' legal guardian. She's spent the past two years living with her son Jack, helping with her grandsons on weekends. Jack had struggled to work after losing an arm in an accident, so Ernst took a job in the special education department of a local school, paid his rent, and spent weekends shopping for the boys and disciplining them "as a mother would." In June, she moved back to Oregon from Connecticut. She needed to help her daughter, Joanna, with her children in the same way she's been helping Jack and his boys. "I wish I could just be a grandmother, but I also discipline, school them, feed them, and provide a home for them," Ernst said. "I enjoy it immensely, but I'm unable to retire, and my retirement money is slowly being spent." For some grandparents, helping adult children through illness, job loss, addiction, or other crises means taking on far more than occasional babysitting. They become the family's financial and practical backstop, spending down savings, delaying retirement, or going back to work to help support both adult children and grandchildren. This year, Business Insider has spoken with more than 60 grandparents and great-grandparents raising young children or helping adult children get back on their feet, just when they thought they'd be retiring. Some have legal custody of their grandchildren. Others, like Ernst, have no official parenting roles but pay bills, provide care, and prepare them for a good life. Census data show that more than 1.1 million US grandparents 60 and older were at least part-time caregivers for their grandchildren as of 2024. "Where is my Barbie?" her older grandson asks. "Barbie is long gone," Ernst replies, adding that she threw her out after her leg fell off. "She's in the city dump." "Can you buy a new Barbie?" "I'll talk about it later with your dad." Ernst raised three children, mostly as a single mother. Around 2016, her daughter Joanna developed a debilitating kidney condition that left her hospitalized for months. Ernst helped care for Joanna's children and received a small state caregiver income. "It never ceases to amaze me how, despite everything, my mom has always been there for my kids and me," Joanna, 43, says. "She always wanted to make us thrive." In 2024, Ernst moved to Connecticut to support Jack after his injury. She found a house with $1,500 monthly rent payments and began her teaching job. Now that she's returned to Oregon, she continues to pay the mortgage on her current house in Connecticut so Jack and his sons can stay there. She also works 25 hours a week as a paid caregiver for Joanna's son with autism and helps to support him financially. Ernst has tried to balance being frugal with the instinct to give her grandchildren small treats, but even going out to the movies can become a budget decision. This isn't what she expected retirement to be. "If you look at a traditional grandparent, they get to have their grandkids for the day, take them out, and give them ice cream," Joann says. "I'm never at that point because I'm constantly disciplining and explaining things. You're never relaxed." Althea Smith, 65, has faced a more formal version of the same pressure. She is raising her grandson as his legal guardian while also providing long-term care for her own parents. Smith has a job as a full-time support worker for older adults and said she doesn't expect to fully retire soon. "I want to see the world and take a cruise," she said. "I miss being able to go wherever I want. My grandson will be 18 in four years, and then I'll be able to think more about myself." Ernst's kitchen table may be filled with receipts and bills — groceries, the mortgage, and a car loan — but she says it's money well-spent. She tries to avoid thinking about her diminishing nest egg. "I know it'll all work out," Joann said, watching the boys dash across the living room.

item.title: Really? Palantir cofounder on AI's threat: 'We’re on top of it’
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.83
Everything's fine! Take it from the cofounder of Palantir. In an X post on Saturday, Joe Lonsdale brushed aside the salient worry that advanced AI systems could cause mass human extinction, a concern that numerous engineers and leaders from frontier AI labs have raised in recent days and weeks. "The world is going to be alright, guys," Lonsdale said. "Leaders have big responsibilities and challenges ahead, but it doesn't help to scare everyone. We are on top of it." That's unlikely enough to calm the nerves of a human population that's been repeatedly told that AI could take control and do all manner of untoward things, including taking everyone's jobs. After Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon quit the company this week and issued dire warnings that frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives," numerous leaders echoed his concern in posts and essays. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a blog post that AI swarms could soon take over the entire internet. He called for more stringent safety regulations and a global, coordinated slowdown on AI development. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis, and Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue all said they agreed with Amodei. Lonsdale? Not so much. Lonsdale is a famously conservative contrarian. He founded the University of Austin in 2021 alongside now-CBS News editor Bari Weiss, which counts "the unhindered pursuit of truth without cancel culture" as one of its core principles. "It's not as much about the politics as it was about being contrarian. I've always relished standing out from the crowd, standing up and disagreeing with everyone," he once told Business Insider in a 2017 interview. The company he helped found and later left, Palantir, builds AI software that helps governments and corporations analyze large amounts of data. The company has several lucrative contracts with the US government. It credited 93% year-over-year revenue growth in Q2 to companies purchasing its enterprise software. In his weekend take that everything's going to be just fine, Lonsdale appears aligned with President Donald Trump. The president has repeatedly scoffed at AI doomerism, emphasizing the need to stay ahead of China in the AI race. In Ireland on Sunday, Trump said AI leaders who have issued warnings about the tech's potential for misuse are "bringing up things that won't happen." "Whoever wins with AI wins," the president told reporters.

item.title: The AI doomsday debate has reached a boiling point
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.54
Existential angst What do you do if you feel like you're helping build something that could contribute to the end of humanity? This is the existential question confronting the AI industry, a debate that only intensified after Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit last week with a stark warning. He said AI giants are "gambling with our lives" and that the people building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." The swift reaction to Coxon's warning boiled over on Saturday when the leaders of the biggest AI companies publicly agreed on what should happen next. In a Saturday essay, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's "become convinced" the breakneck pace of advancement must change and proposed a three-step solution to ensure the tech's safety. Shortly afterward, Elon Musk and Sam Altman publicly aligned with Amodei's plan in a rare sign of support. "Dario is right," Musk tweeted. Altman agreed, too, saying the pace of development has been a "primary topic" of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks. Altman also said OpenAI might not move forward with an IPO this year. "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," he said in a Fortune interview. As fears over AI safety intensify, employees at Anthropic and OpenAI have also been speaking out. My colleague Sarah Needleman reported on a big question facing many concerned AI employees: Should they quit or stay amid fears of an AI apocalypse? Some AI workers believe they can do more good by staying on the inside. That means raising concerns, pushing for safeguards, and trying to influence decisions before they are made. Others worry that staying at these companies only helps legitimize a race that some believe is getting dangerously out of control. BI's Alistair Bar explored some of these theories in this week's edition of AI Insider — you can subscribe here to his weekly newsletter. Are employees at the big AI lab companies better off leaving or staying if they feel like their work is contributing to a possible AI apocalypse? Send me a note at srussolillo@businessinsider.com and let me know what you think.

item.title: Read the memo: CBS News leadership is selling staffers on '60 Minutes' as it relaunches under Bari Weiss
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.28
CBS News is getting employees hyped about the first full season of "60 Minutes" under top editor Bari Weiss, months after a string of high-profile exits. "We don't often send notes to the whole newsroom. But today calls for it. It's a big moment for 60 Minutes and CBS," newsroom leaders, including Weiss, wrote about the new "60 Minutes" season in a memo sent to staffers on Sunday. The memo teases an interview — that "everyone has been chasing" — with a US Air Force officer who was rescued from Iran in April. The 59th season of "60 Minutes" will have 10 regular contributors, including five correspondents: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Jon Wertheim, Norah O'Donnell, and Ross Douthat, who joined CBS from The New York Times in July. "60 Minutes" is kicking off its highly anticipated season following a turbulent early-summer stretch for the storied news program. Lead producer Nick Bilton, who was handpicked by Weiss in May, started his tenure by firing longtime correspondent Scott Pelley after a noisy confrontation in front of "60 Minutes" staffers. Pelley had publicly questioned Bilton's qualifications, pressed his new boss on why fellow correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were let go, and accused Weiss of "murdering" the iconic Sunday night telecast while trying to "kill" CBS News. Weiss later addressed the firing, telling staffers she's "only interested in working in a newsroom that is built on trust and mutual respect." Bilton told "60 Minutes" employees that his first week had been "a trying and difficult few days." Veteran correspondents Whitaker, Wertheim, and Stahl — who's been with "60" since 1991 — decided to return to the program, saying that they "don't want to see 60 Minutes die." They said they're "working to build trust" with Bilton and "heard all the right things" in his memo. "If we can continue doing the work that made this show what it is — committing acts of independent, fearless journalism and storytelling — we're here for it. If not, we leave," Stahl, Whitaker, and Wertheim wrote in their memo. Read the full memo sent to CBS News staffers here: All -- We don't often send notes to the whole newsroom. But today calls for it. It's a big moment for 60 Minutes and CBS. Ahead of our premiere, we wanted to congratulate the team on the launch of what will be an exciting season—and to thank everyone across the CBS newsroom. Tonight's episode is a powerful start with three original, revelatory stories that showcase 60 at its best. We begin with the interview everyone has been chasing. Then, a hidden camera investigation and a profile of a NFL superteam's wunderkind coach. We also have a cameo from one of our new correspondents on the story of our time: AI. We are deeply thankful to everyone across CBS News for the support over this summer. That especially goes for social, digital, graphics, marketing, and, above all, the investigative unit. Last but not least: You've probably seen the great "It's Time" campaign everywhere. That push continues through tonight's game. We'd be grateful if you can spread the word to your friends and followers by sharing these promos today. This is just the start and there's so much more to come. See you tonight at 7:30pm! Nick, Bari, and Tom

item.title: Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.84
On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions. But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. "What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage and possibly drone operations and related disruptions." Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party. In a recent interview with DW, she complained, "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table." She accuses the German government of failing to take action. "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong." Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel. Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior." In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety or violate environmental regulations. Russia's threats: just a bluff? It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint aims to avoid escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war." Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded. "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened," Peters said. "Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely avoided confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels." After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through." Armed Russian crews on board Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk. "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board," Pawlak said. "Those are risks that must be factored into the equation." Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way. "It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel." Inspections would raise costs for Russia While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone," he said. "Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it." He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy." This article has been translated from German. What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

item.title: BRICS summit leaders urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.28
What you need to know This blog is now closed. Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from the BRICS Summit 2026 in India on September 12 and 13, 2026: - Indian PM Modi has announced the adoption of a joint declaration - The BRICS coalition expressed concern over escalations in the Middle East - Modi will meet China's Xi on the sidelines of BRICS today - Putin and Modi discuss a wide range of issues, including the Ukraine-Russia conflict, energy cooperation and trade across several sectors - Modi again urges Putin to end the war in Ukraine - Modi calls for maritime trade to be protected during bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New Delhi - Pezeshkian warns Iran coming under 'critical, dangerous' US economic pressure Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. Thank you for following our coverage This blog is now closed. Catch up on all that happened with our updates blow. What to know: Five key takeaways from the BRICS Summit in Delhi, from DW's Head of Geopolitics Here are five main takeaways from the 18th BRICS Summit in Delhi. 1. The New Delhi Declaration The 45-page declaration has a paragraph on the Iran war. It expresses "deep concern" over the escalation in the Middle East and calls for “maximum restraint." No country is named or blamed. That’s BRICS diplomacy — and the only wording the diverse bloc could agree on. The war directly involves three BRICS members — Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia — which are on opposite sides of the conflict. It took careful diplomacy and night shifts to get even this wording over the finishing line. Still, it is arguably better than nothing — especially with all three countries represented in the room, and China offering a mediating role for BRICS. Whether anything tangible comes from it remains to be seen. 2. The notable absence of Ukraine Ukraine is not mentioned once in the Delhi declaration. That is different from the BRICS declaration in Rio last year, which at least referred to members' "national positions concerning the conflict in Ukraine." But even then, Russia was not named, its invasion was not condemned and there was no call for Russian troops to withdraw. For Putin, the total omission now is politically useful — especially since he was in Delhi, unlike in Rio. 3. Modi meets Xi Xi Jinping has not visited India since 2019. Relations froze after a deadly clash along their disputed Himalayan border in 2020. His meeting with Modi in Delhi marks another step in a cautious thaw between the two nuclear-armed Asian powers and perhaps also sends a signal to Washington. Both Modi and Xi want a more multipolar world and less Western dominance of the global financial system. But they are coming at it from very different positions. China is already the world’s second-largest economy, with a powerful and assertive military. Its focus is on countering Washington. India, meanwhile, is pursuing multi-alignment and strategic autonomy building ties with Russia, the US and the EU for different reasons, without moving into China’s camp. Mistrust remains, especially over the contested border and who gets to shape Asia. India’s huge trade deficit with China adds another layer. 4. The T-factor Donald Trump was the elephant in the room. But neither he nor the United States is named in the Delhi declaration. They are there nonetheless: BRICS leaders condemn unilateral sanctions and voice concern over unilateral tariffs. So there are shared frustrations with the Western-dominated global order and Trump’s tactics. But the wars in Iran and Ukraine also expose the limits of BRICS’ strategic cohesion. 5."Greater BRICS" China was key to expanding BRICS from five to 11 members. Xi now wants to pull the larger BRICS family closer together — through cooperation on future technologies, industries and resilient supply chains. The idea is to turn the expanded BRICS into a more integrated Global South network — technologically and, eventually, geopolitically. India will now hand the BRICS chairmanship to China and will be watching closely. Like China, India wants BRICS to give the Global South more voice. But it does not want BRICS to become a China-led anti-Western alliance. That is the tension at the heart of BRICS. A bigger BRICS does not necessarily mean a more cohesive BRICS.
BRICS: How a four-nation group became a global bloc Interestingly, BRICS as we know it today did not start as a formal economic or geopolitical coalition; it rather started as an economic acronym coined by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill in 2001. O'Neill, in his investment paper, grouped Brazil, Russia, India, and China based on their rapid growth potential. He argued these economies would collectively dominate the global economy by 2050. The identification of these economies triggered a massive influx of foreign capital investment into these specific countries, and soon the political leadership of these countries realized that the world viewed them as a unified economic bloc. In 2006, the foreign ministers of Brazil, Russia, India and China met for the first time on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The formal diplomatic coalition was officially established at their first official summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009. BRIC became BRICS when South Africa joined the bloc in 2010. The 2023 summit in Johannesburg marked a historic turn for the bloc when it extended formal invitations to six new nations. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates officially joined the bloc, however, Argentina's new government declined membership in late 2023. In 2025, Indonesia became the latest country to join the bloc, making BRICS an eleven member-strong bloc which has increasingly positioned itself as the voice of the Global South. Besides the 11 members, BRICS also has 10 partner countries. Modi warns against 'weaponization' of technology, critical minerals In his opening address on Day 2 of the BRICS Summit in Delhi, Modi warned the "weaponization of technology and critical minerals" could hinder global development and shared prosperity. He said rising geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions and climate crises are increasingly affecting people worldwide and called for strengthened cooperation and support across the Global South. Xi pushes for 'Greater BRICS' economic cooperation Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sunday announced initiatives in areas ranging from AI to trade to deepen cooperation among the "Greater BRICS" emerging economies. It comes as Beijing seeks to transform the bloc into a practical platform for Global South development. The success of the "Greater BRICS Initiative" depends on laying a solid foundation for pragmatic cooperation, Xi told the leaders' annual summit in New Delhi, the official Xinhua news agency said. 'Greater BRICS' nations should improve cooperation, maintain the stability of industrial and supply chains, and cultivate an integrated market, Xi told the summit's closing session. China and Russia describe the expanded bloc — which now has 11 countries as its members — as "Greater BRICS." China will take the initiative of establishing a BRICS AI Open Source Zone to promote cooperation on large language models, AI training and an open AI ecosystem, Xi added. Russia says Modi, Xi offered to mediate Ukraine peace talks: State media Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had both offered their services for peace talks on Ukraine, state news agency TASS reported. The agency added that Russian President Vladimir Putin had welcomed India and China's readiness. The three leaders are among those attending the BRICS summit in Delhi. Welcome back to our coverage We are resuming our coverage of the BRICS Summit 2026, taking place in New Delhi at the Bharat Mandapam. The first day of the summit concluded with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announcing the adoption of a joint declaration by the BRICS bloc. The 45-page declaration called for condemnation of terrorism, conflict prevention and peaceful resolution of disputes. The bloc also called for reforms in the UN, including its Security Council "with a view to making it more democratic, representative, effective and efficient, and to increase the representation of developing countries in the Council's membership." Iran and US ally United Arab Emirates also signed up to the joint statement that called for restraint in the Middle East war. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi on the sidelines of the first day of the New Delhi summit, in the countries' highest-level meeting since the start of the conflict. Meanwhile, Modi held a bilateral meeting with China's Xi Jinping, who was visiting the country for the first time since India-China relations nosedived in 2020 after a deadly clash over border disputes in Ladakh's Galwan Valley. Modi also held bilateral meetings with the leaders of Iran, Ethiopia and Abu Dhabi. Stay tuned as we bring you more from the second and last day of the 18th BRICS Summit. Thank you for following our coverage We are now pausing our coverage of the BRICS summit in New Delhi. We will be back on Sunday, September 13, with more headlines. Xi calls for promotion of 'financial cooperation' with India Chinese President Xi Jinping called for Beijing to strengthen its financial cooperation with India during a visit to New Delhi for a BRICS summit. "Both sides should… work hand-in-hand to promote high-quality major financial cooperation, advocate an equal and sustainable global order, and foster an economic globalization that is open and inclusive," Xi said. Meanwhile, the Indian Foreign Ministry said that he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi "underlined the need to address each other's concerns, including structural trade imbalance and supply chain issues, and facilitation of meaningful and predictable market access." China is India's largest trading partner, with bilateral goods reaching $151 billion (€130 billion) in the financial year of 2025-26. During this period, India imported $131 billion of goods from China, while India exported some $19 billion worth of goods to its neighbor. India, China to work towards resolving disputed border — New Delhi India and China have "expressed commitment" to normalizing their disputed border, India's Foreign Ministry said. "The two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question," the ministry said as Chinese President Xi Jinping visits New Delhi for a BRICS summit. The ministry added the Prime Minister Narendra Modi "underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border related issues." "Differences should not become disputes," it said. The statement said that Modi stressed that China and India both "must be guided by three mutuals — mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest." Both India and China maintain heavy military deployments along their 3,500 kilometer (2,175-mile) border along Kashmir and Tibet. Chinese and Indian troops engaged in several skirmishes along the disputed border in 2020 and 2021. China 'willing to work with fellow BRICS members' towards achieving Middle East peace, says Xi Speaking at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping called for greater efforts to promote peace in the Middle East and the Gulf region. "China is willing to work with fellow BRICS members to play due role in achieving peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region," President Xi Jinping told the official Xinhua news agency in New Delhi. "The war has caused serious losses to people across the region and does not serve the common interests of the international community," Xi added, according to Xinhua. Xi also pointed out that power politics are on the rise, the international order is being challenged and there are growing shortcomings in terms of peace and security. The BRICS nations must stand "on the right side of history," he urged. What does the joint declaration say? On the first day of the BRICS Summit, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the adoption of a joint declaration. The joint declaration adopted by the BRICS coalition calls for "maximum restraint" in the Middle East. "We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," the statement read. The member states have reiterated their commitment to peaceful resolution of international disputes through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy. The declaration also advocates for a multilateral approach that respects diverse national viewpoints and positions on crucial global issues. The declaration comes at a time when the US and Iran have resumed tit-for-tat strikes against each other, after a pause in fighting for much of August. Since the bloc inlcuded Iran and US-ally UAE both, it was expected that reaching a concensus will be difficult. Additionally, the bloc expressed concerns about the rise of "unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures" that distort trade, against the backdrop of US sanctions against Tehran amid its war with the country, and against Russia over its conflict with Ukraine. The bloc stressed on the need to cooperate to maintain the smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy. What does a joint declaration against war mean for the bloc's influence? "It’s all done," Indian prime minister Narendra Modi said. And what he meant was this: BRICS has an approved joint declaration for 2026. The leaders agreed on the text of the Delhi Declaration on day one of the summit after their plenary session. It is important to keep in mind that, for the first six months of the Iran war, the grouping of Global South nations failed to issue a joint statement. The US-Israel-led attack on Iran has put enormous strain on the bloc. The war directly involves three BRICS members: Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. But not as allies. Iran has attacked the UAE and Saudi Arabia, seeing them as proxies for the US. The war has been devastating for the Global South, which BRICS represents. Think oil and fertilizers — and food security. The compromise now found in Delhi appears to be a joint declaration condemning unilateral wars, without naming any country. That is rather low-key — but perhaps better than nothing, especially for BRICS chair India, which can claim this as a diplomatic victory. As former UN diplomat and prominent Indian foreign policy voice Shashi Tharoor had told me before the summit: "There is very little doubt that all the BRICS members have not necessarily upheld the UN Charter, the inviolability of borders, the sovereignty of member states of the UN, and the inadmissibility of the use of force to settle international disputes." The BRICS countries now number 11 and represent about half of the world’s population. And when economies are measured by what people can actually buy, they account for around 40 percent of global economic output. So BRICS leaders feel they have a strong case for criticizing western political hegemony and the dominance of the US dollar. They argue that global institutions such as the UN, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank no longer reflect the rising power of emerging economies and the Global South. In his opening address, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that reform of the UN Security Council cannot wait any longer. Xi says US-Iran war doesn't serve "common interests": Xinhua Speaking during the BRICS Summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping said that the Middle East war, sparked by US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, does not serve the world's interests, Beijing's state media reported. "As the situation in the Middle East and the Gulf region continues to evolve, the war there has caused serious losses to people across the region," state news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying in New Delhi, which is hosting the 18th BRICS summit attended by leaders including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. It "does not serve the common interests of the international community", Xi said, according to Xinhua. BRICS reaches consensus, Modi announces joint declaration In his closing remarks for the first session at the BRICS Summit, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the BRICS group of nations unanimously adopted a joint declaration on Saturday, the first day of their annual summit in New Delhi. Reuters news agency, citing four anonymous sources, had earlier in the day reported that members of the BRICS coalition have agreed on a joint declaration which does not name any country but will condemn unilateral war by any country. The members include Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

item.title: Cyberattack in Berlin: 1.4 million files on the dark web
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.52
It was a story that almost went unnoticed amid all the clamor surrounding the closely watched state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. This highly alarming story is one of many recent reports that have detailed attacks on infrastructure or drone attacks on airports carried out by hostile foreign powers. Incidents like this one in the German capital highlight just how vulnerable Germany's data networks are. So what exactly happened? Since early September, employee files, official correspondence, pay stubs and even scanned ID documents have been appearing on the dark web. The hacker group Rhysida stole the data and then tried to extort the Berlin city government. They demanded a ransom of 30 bitcoins, which is equivalent to about €2 million ($2.3 million), or else they would publish the sensitive data. But last Friday, Berlin's Governing Mayor Kai Wegner stated: "The State of Berlin will not give in to blackmail." The data was subsequently published on the dark web, the part of the internet accessible only to tech-savvy users, where a lot of illegal activity takes place. In total, the data set consists of approximately 1.4 million records. An employee unknowingly opened a phishing email Two departments of the city government serving approximately four million residents have been compromised: the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transportation. This time, the attack wasn't carried out by foreign intelligence agencies, but by criminals. The hackers initially gained access to protected data between August 7 and 14 without being detected. Rhysida, a cybercrime group believed to originate from eastern Europe, has been attacking public institutions around the world since 2023, claiming responsibility for nearly 280 attacks, primarily in the US. The hackers were able to gain access when a Berlin Transportation Authority employee replied to a phishing email, a message disguised to appear genuine and benign. Opening one of the attachments inadvertently grants the attackers access to the victim's network. In Berlin, the state government's secure fiber-optic network connects approximately 600 locations, ranging from municipal offices to senate departments. Data disclosure could have serious consequences The list of sectors that experts believe could be compromised illustrates the real gravity of the data breach. In addition to the personal data of employees and citizens, this includes information on combi-heat and power plants, fuel storage facilities, emergency power supply systems as well as prisons and water treatment plants. In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, Jochim Selzer of the Chaos Computer Club said that the publication could have serious consequences for the people affected — even if the data only appeared on the hard-to-access dark web: "The more you know about a person, the better you can impersonate them and the better you can figure out what you need to know about them in order to, say, place an order on their behalf." Is changing passwords enough? And what about the political authorities responsible? The Berlin state government has instructed its employees to change their passwords. That, however, sparked outrage from Thorsten Schleheider, the vice-chairman of Berlin's police union. He said that Berlin's data has been inadequately protected for years and that many employees have not received sufficient training: "It is unthinkable that highly sensitive data was compromised for days, and the only action taken appears to be instructing employees to change their passwords." To address the data breach, the Berlin Senate has set up a coordination office involving all Berlin administrative agencies. It has also established contact with federal agencies such as the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), based in Bonn. Mayor Kai Wegner said, "We will inform, advise and support those employees and Berliners who were affected as quickly as possible." Berlin state elections on September 20 remain safe The Berlin authorities were, however, able to provide reassurance regarding at least one issue of concern. They announced that the September 20 election for the Berlin State Parliament is not at risk. State Election Commissioner Stephan Bröchler told the Bild tabloid: "As things stand, all systems and processes necessary for the election remain unaffected — including election preparations, the actual election day itself and the steps leading up to the release of the preliminary results." Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was at least indirectly affected by the data theft. The stolen information also includes details about the controversial expansion of the Chancellery in the heart of Berlin. This article was translated from German.

item.title: France: Attack ruled out in train derailment
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.38
A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, authorities said. The public prosecutor of Rouen, Sebastian Gallois, said Saturday evening that there was "no indication of a malicious act carried out with the deliberate intention of derailing the train, and certainly not of an attack," according to reports in the French media. Gallois' remarks came after some politicians had suggested earlier on Saturday that the incident might have been the result of sabotage or other criminal activity.
