At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement. One of the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added. Her condition has reportedly improved in the hours since. The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said. What else do we know about the train derailment? French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene. Local authorities had urged the public to avoid the area. The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended. "The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said. A police spokesperson had said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object. A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports. Edited by: Wesley Dockery If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.20
In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members. "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind. "It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW. For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible. "India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there." Why India's role at the BRICS summit matters Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil. At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing. "The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa. She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member. For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship. However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend. "In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh. Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first". However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times. "With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole. "India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?" Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned. "India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics." What is BRICS for anyway? BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose. The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP. Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order. "Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa. She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues. There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh. What could the BRICS summit achieve? Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security. While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO. "India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely." Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm." He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve. "With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

item.title: Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.89
Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze. The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast. "Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly." The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain. Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday. "We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said. No deaths reported in blaze Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated. No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released. Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency. Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment. Firefighting planes active on the scene As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area. Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze. Edited by: Natalie Muller If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.63
At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday. The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 miles) east of Australia. The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities. The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae. Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea." Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials. In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts move toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors." "To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of those missing and those we have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," the statement continued. Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui. "This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel." Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized." French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted. It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor. "He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge. "There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added. Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own. The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort. A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning. The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning. Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island. Edited by: Natalie Muller If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Russia's drone war comes to Moldova and Romania
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.17
For Ukrainians, Russia's air war has been a bitter, bloody reality for years. People in Ukraine are being killed every day by missiles, bombs, and drones. But the country's central and southeastern European neighbors have also found themselves affected, albeit on a smaller scale: Missiles and drones sometimes invade their air space, and occasionally even crash on their territory. Now the Russian drone war is coming dangerously close to two of Ukraine's neighbors: Romania and the Republic of Moldova, where drone incidents are now an almost daily occurrence. The drones often explode, leaving people injured, and there have also been recent attacks on Ukrainian checkpoints at the Moldovan and Romanian borders. The attacks have now escalated to such a degree that many observers believe they can no longer be considered unintentional. They suspect the Kremlin is deliberately trying to bring the war to Ukraine's neighbors. The latest drone incursion and crash on Tuesday caused a furore as it prevented a plane with the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on board from taking off in the Moldovan capital Chisinau. A Russian Geran drone, which can fly as fast as 500 kilometers per hour (311 mph), took off in Crimea, then flew through Ukrainian airspace and eventually crashed in a sunflower field near the Moldovan city of Riscani. The drone also flew over Romania, where two fighter jets were scrambled from NATO's Kogalniceanu airbase near the Black Sea port of Constanta, though it remains unclear why they did not shoot down the drone, as they had on other occasions. More and more incidents in Moldova and Romania The most serious aspect of the incident was that it showed how limited Moldovan air defense is in its ability to protect the country's air space. The drones were detected and tracked by air traffic control, but it was not possible to shoot them down. According to publicly available information, the country possesses only a small number of Polish Piorun anti-aircraft missiles, and these are only able to protect certain specific targets. There have been around three dozen drone incidents in Romania and Moldova since the beginning of August this year. The majority were airspace violations, but there have also been crashes and explosions, while debris has also been found. In Romania, several drones have also been shot down. According to official data, 17 drones crashed in August in Moldova alone – as many as in all of 2025. Deaths at border crossings There was also a drone strike on the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and southeastern Moldova on the night of September 8. The crossing, situated around a kilometer from Moldovan territory, and was damaged in the attack. Two people were killed and two others wounded, one of them a Moldovan citizen. The Moldovan leadership has strongly condemned the drone attack. President Maia Sandu said on Wednesday that Russia's war had arrived at the Moldovan border. "It is hard to understand, given this reality, that there are still voices who try to convince Moldovans that Russia is not the aggressor, or that the war in our part of the world has nothing to do with us," Sandu said. The president of the Moldovan parliament, Igor Grosu, wrote on Facebook that these were incidents "we can no longer view as something remote." The threat from Russia, Grosu said, was not a "specter," and not propaganda: "It is a daily reality." Moldova's Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatii said that the deaths of Moldovan citizens could no longer be ruled out in future. Vladimir Bolea, the minister of infrastructure, warned that Giurgiulesti, Moldova's port on the Danube, could become a target after the Russian Foreign Ministry accused Romania and Moldova of using the port as a "transit hub" for arms shipments. 'Planned operation' by Russia? Moldovan military and security expert Rosian Vasiloi, a former head of the Moldovan border police, wrote on Facebook in response to Tuesday's drone crash in Moldova: "This is a planned operation by the aggressor state." He also referred to the drone's peculiar flight path: After flying from Ukraine over Moldova into Romania, it made an about-turn and flew back to Moldova. Vasiloi concluded: "We can no longer view our airspace as separate from Ukraine's and Romania's. Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, and Romania already form an interconnected operational area as far as air threats and their impact on regional connectivity are concerned." The Romanian leadership has not yet reacted to the latest incidents. But in July, the Romanian government made a political and military change of course: After a long period of restraint, it started to shoot down drones in Romanian airspace. Former Romanian General Virgil Balaceanu, a regular analyst in the country's media, has urged Romania's leaders to accelerate the enhancement of Romanian air defenses. Balaceanu also believes that the drone incident on Tuesday was a deliberate maneuver. Following this latest incident, the US Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a leading public think tank for analysis of Russia's war against Ukraine, wrote that while there was no evidence that the airspace violations were intentional, it could be said that Russia benefited from such actions. In particular, it wrote, the incursions using Russia's latest, extremely fast Geran drone model "aim to further test NATO and Moldovan defenses and the response of the entire NATO alliance." This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Russian GRU spies behind failed Leipzig attack: reports
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.85
Germany's Welt am Sonntag (WaS) newspaper has cited intelligence reports tying the recent failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport directly to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency. In an article published on Saturday, Welt am Sonntag said that a man with known ties to the GRU was responsible for operational logistics in the attempted attack. Further, it said those ties were known to German authorities when the man entered the country from Turkey, nevertheless, he was not surveilled after arrival. Classified security assessments cited by the paper say the Russian national is now in his home country after departing to Serbia on a flight from Berlin-Brandenburg Airport. A second man, a Belarus citizen, was also cited as an accomplice in the report. Explosives thought to have entered Germany from Bulgaria and Serbia German intelligence sources said that the explosives used in the incident were likely smuggled into Germany via truck from Bulgaria and Serbia and then stored in underground depots once they arrived in Leipzig. Berlin quickly made clear that forensic evidence found at Leipzig/Halle Airport — including drone configuration, explosives and trigger mechanisms used in other Russian hybrid attacks — pointed to a Russian plot. In early August, German tabloid BILD reported that authorities had found DNA traces on the drone's remote control antenna. Those samples were said to have matched DNA found at the scene of a July 20, 2024, arson attack at a Leipzig logistics facility operated by German courier company DHL. Leipzig attack averted but Russian escalation will continue The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport — a hub for military aid destined for Ukraine — occurred on the evening of August 4 and involved an explosives-laden drone that was found near a Ukrainian transport jet. Authorities were able to disarm the drone and after public speculation that Moscow was behind the incident the German government officially blamed Russia in early September. Saturday's article said Berlin made the attribution on the basis of the intelligence reports cited. In response to its conclusion, Germany announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn. The Kremlin in turn reacted by closing Goethe Institutes — a German cultural exchange outfit — across Russia. As in numerous similar hybrid attacks prior, Russia has denied any involvement in the incident. Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Werner Herzog: Germany's wild man of cinema is back
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.61
When Werner Herzog needed a title for his memoirs, he reached back to one of his own films: "Every Man for Himself and God Against All," the original German title of his 1974 feature known in English as "The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser." For Herzog, perhaps the last wild man of European cinema, it's less a title than a worldview. Over more than 60 years as a provocative, boundary-breaking filmmaker, Herzog has made films on the slopes of active volcanoes, and in the middle of the Sahara. He's filmed in the jungle and north of the Arctic Circle, telling stories of characters who live at the edges of human achievement. Often, in making these films, Herzog has pushed himself, and his collaborators, to the edge as well. Now 84, Werner Herzog shows no signs of slowing down. He's back with a new feature film, "Bucking Fastard," his first drama in seven years, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival. 'Bucking Fastard:' two sisters, totally in sync The film is the story of Jean and Joan Holbrooke, two sisters who speak, think and move in unison. They even share the same dreams and love the same undeserving man. Hollywood stars and real-life siblings Kate and Rooney Mara play the sisters, their performances synced up to an uncanny degree. The film is loosely inspired by real-life twin sisters Freda and Greta Chaplin, who became a tabloid sensation in England in the 1980s. The film's title is a reference to an inadvertent simultaneous spoonerism the sisters made in court, when describing their former lover. In Herzog's version, the Holbrooke sisters, after being rejected by their true love (played by Orlando Bloom), decamp to the wilds of Ireland and begin digging a tunnel in a cave, convinced they can dig their way to the Orkney Islands — a mythical place where true love is possible. Reaching out for the extraordinary The Holbrooke sisters are two ecstatic dreamers striving to do the impossible. Typical Herzog protagonists. Herzog himself sees the through-line. "With 'Fitzcarraldo,' there is a great dream about opera in the jungle, and for that the protagonist moves a big ship over a mountain," he told DW in Venice. Herzog was referring to his 1982 epic adventure drama in which he had his crew actually haul a 320-ton steamship over a hill in the Peruvian jungle to tell the story of a man who dreams of building an opera house in the middle of the rainforest. Similarly, added the director, "Bucking Fastard" is "the dream of an ideal country, which doesn't really exist." In the world of Werner Herzog, art imitates life, and vice versa. While filming "Aguirre, the Wrath of God" (1972), the story of a mad conquistador in search of El Dorado, Herzog and his crew, including star Klaus Kinski, nearly went mad themselves. In his 1999 documentary on Kinski, "My Best Fiend," Herzog recounts how the actor threatened to leave the film. If he did, the director told him, he would follow him and shoot him dead. Real people, real extremes Herzog is, if anything, even better known as a documentarian and his real-life protagonists are as extreme as his fictional characters. In "Grizzly Man" (2005), he ponders the life of Timothy Treadwell, an animal rights activist who spent years getting up close and personal with bears in the wild, until one of them ate him. "Little Dieter Needs to Fly" (1997) follows the German-born American Vietnam War pilot Dieter Dengler, who survived a harrowing escape from a Laotian prison camp. For "La Soufriere" (1977), Herzog filmed in an abandoned town in Guadeloupe, next to a volcano on the brink of eruption, to talk to the one man who refuses to evacuate. Films as our 'collective dreams' Herzog sees little difference between his fiction and non-fiction films. He admits to inventing scenes for his documentaries, and to filming real events for his features. For "Rescue Dawn" (2006), a feature adaptation of the Dieter Dengler story, Herzog got star Christian Bale to devour live maggots on camera (the director showed him how, gobbling up some himself) and wrestle with a real live snake for a scene. "Film does not have so much to do with reality as it does with our collective dreams," Herzog said. He thinks of himself less as a director than "as a poet." 'Just go out and do it' In his often haunting tales of man's struggle with nature, Herzog aims to achieve an "ecstatic truth" beyond mere reality. His goal, he said, is not to depict the extreme as bizarre or extraordinary. It is to inspire everyone to be extraordinary. "Every grown-up man should move a ship over a mountain. Every grown-up woman should dig a tunnel through a mountain range," he told DW. "[The message] is very simple: Just go out and do it." Rooney Mara agreed: "Being willing to show up every day and dig a tunnel through a mountain for love — that's not crazy. Everyone else is crazy for not wanting to do that." A divided response in Venice "Bucking Fastard" is an odd, and oddly funny film, especially for a Herzog movie. "Thank you for seeing that," said Herzog, who argued there is humor in all his films, if you look for it. "Sometimes it's a dark humor. Sometimes it's a very Bavarian humor that even Germans wouldn't understand. For Americans, it's easier. Mexicans, yes, they immediately get it." The Venice audience gave "Bucking Fastard" a warm welcome, but critics were more divided. A few embraced Herzog's new piece of ecstatic weirdness. Most dismissed it as confusing, clunky and utterly nonsensical. An "uddled-mup fairytale," wrote one, playing on the film's mixed up title. Why Herzog still matters Herzog critics are legion, but his fans probably don't care. The 84-year-old director is as popular as he's ever been. He launched an Instagram account last year, even though he still doesn't own a smartphone, and it has become a huge hit with Gen Z. "My younger son does it, he knows how, and he tells me 85% of those who read it and love it are between 15 and 20 years old," Herzog said. "And because my films are now available on the internet, on streaming platforms, all of a sudden [young people] are discovering it." Mara said Herzog remains an inspiration, as "a singular human being [who] really doesn't give a sh**." Speaking to the German director, she noted: "You march to the beat of your own drum so thoroughly, and people love that because that's what we all want to do." Next stop: outer space? For his part, Herzog is not slowing down. He's already put "Bucking Fastard" behind him and is deep in post-production on his new film and has a Taschen photo book in progress. And he still hasn't given up on his impossible dream: making a film in space. "I spoke to NASA, but they didn't take me. And then there is a Japanese billionaire who is planning a spaceship around the moon [but] he refused to take me on board," he said. "[But] Elon Musk promised me that if he goes on a mission to Mars, I would be on board." Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

item.title: The Emerging U.S.-China Détente
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 5.47
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump met in Beijing, in May, they agreed that their two countries should build a constructive relationship of strategic stability. Although many observers in Washington responded skeptically to this new framework, dismissing it as empty words, it marks the first time in more than a decade that China and the United States established a consensus about how to define the relationship that leaders on both sides broadly recognize. Strategic stability does not refer to nuclear détente; rather, it suggests a new equilibrium in which both sides can avoid further deterioration of the relationship and even expand cooperation where interests align. Leaders in Beijing do not expect that this new framework can resolve most of the differences between China and the United States or that it can stop new frictions from emerging. In June, for example, the U.S. Department of Defense placed more Chinese companies—including private-sector giants Alibaba, Baidu, and BYD—on its list of firms involved in civil-military fusion activities, barring the Pentagon from contracting with them. In retaliation, China placed ten U.S. entities on its dual-use export control list, which prevents any company from supplying them with items that have the potential for both military and civilian use. But Beijing hopes that a consensus built around strategic stability can help China and the United States manage their differences more effectively and that it will prevent the worst outcomes: military conflict or a new cold war. So far, ongoing friction has not derailed the overarching consensus established in May. By keeping sanctions and countermeasures relatively limited, Beijing and Washington have avoided dangerous escalation and kept the relationship moving forward. The goal of the new diplomatic framework between Beijing and Washington is a pragmatic one. It aims to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations rather than try to achieve an unlikely grand bargain that would resolve all conflict. It also represents a changing approach in Beijing to dealing with the United States. Unlike in the past, when China rejected U.S. frameworks focused on competition, it is now willing to recognize that the fundamental nature of U.S.-Chinese relations is competitive. Allies or partners, after all, would not set strategic stability as the overarching goal of their relationship; only competitors, or even adversaries, need to do so. Beijing’s willingness to accept a formulation to manage, rather than exclude, competition shows that it is gaining confidence and seeing itself more as an equal to Washington. Adopting this confident mindset could lead China to act with more restraint in its dealings with the United States—which could in turn bring a further degree of calm to the relationship. It now appears plausible that bilateral relations have turned a corner and entered a more stable phase. Although fundamental challenges remain that could cause new turbulence, the peak tensions of the past eight years may well be receding. The upcoming leaders’ summit in late September, when Xi and Trump are scheduled to meet in Washington, is a chance to further move the relationship forward. The two leaders can now add more concrete measures to support this new framework of strategic stability, including taking steps to reduce economic friction, increase military-to-military communications, improve crisis management mechanisms, expand citizen exchanges, and offer reassurances about Taiwan, thereby defusing tensions that could escalate into potentially catastrophic military conflict. With Xi and Trump likely to meet again multiple times in the next few months, the new framework is the first chance in years to lay the groundwork for enduring stability in bilateral ties. BEYOND STRATEGIC COMPETITION For a long time, leaders in both Beijing and Washington sought to define the bilateral relationship in terms of some kind of partnership. In 1997, when Chinese leader Jiang Zemin visited the United States, Beijing and Washington announced aims of “a constructive strategic partnership oriented toward the twenty-first century.” In 2005, the George W. Bush administration urged China “to become a responsible stakeholder” in the international system; Chinese leader Hu Jintao responded in 2006 that the two countries were not only stakeholders but “should also be constructive partners.” But between 2009, when President Barack Obama and Hu agreed to “steadily grow a partnership” to address common challenges, and the Trump-Xi summit earlier this year, the countries’ leaders were unable to reach a new consensus on how to position the relationship. The United States moved away from seeing the relationship as a partnership earlier than China did. During Trump’s first term, the United States began to define U.S.-Chinese relations in terms of “strategic competition.” At first, China tried to accept the competitive element in bilateral relations. Beijing acknowledged that some competition was inevitable while hoping that the relationship could remain positive overall. But as U.S.-Chinese relations deteriorated sharply in the final year of Trump’s first term and continued to worsen into the Biden administration, Beijing began to see “strategic competition” as a narrative designed to foreclose China’s rise. It felt that the U.S. approach threatened its development prospects, leading Beijing to push back more forcefully against the concept. In July 2022, during a phone call with President Joe Biden, Xi told his counterpart that it was a mistake to make competition the defining feature of the relationship. To policymakers and analysts in China, the framework of strategic competition turned all U.S.-Chinese interactions into something akin to the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. They saw the United States’ actions such as export controls on semiconductors as concrete manifestations that the United States was trying to suppress China, to undercut its political system, and to constrain its development. Although official statements from Washington discussed bilateral ties in terms of cooperation, competition, and confrontation, in practice competition and confrontation snuffed out any potential for cooperation. After almost a decade in which China rejected and criticized strategic competition, transitioning to a relationship of constructive strategic stability reflects Beijing’s recalibrated assessment of both countries’ positions and roles in the international system, as well as the new realities of U.S.-Chinese relations. China is looking at bilateral relations from a position of greater equality and with more confidence, and it is less anxious that competition will undermine its national development prospects. Instead, Beijing believes that competition can be effectively managed without presenting an existential threat. MORE THAN ONE MAN Whether strategic stability succeeds as the basis of a new phase in U.S.-Chinese relations depends on whether it is rooted in the personal wills and agendas of Trump and Xi or it arises from structural forces that are more powerful than any individual leader. Many observers in both Beijing and Washington view the emerging consensus as a contingent result of the interests of the two men currently in charge. Trump, for instance, has taken it upon himself to change the direction of U.S. policy. His unexpected turn toward embracing a more stable relationship with China coincides with other unexpected turns in his second-term agenda, including adopting a cold and even hostile attitude toward European allies and launching a war against Iran despite frequently decrying U.S. military involvement overseas. But these shifts also obscure more durable structural factors in the U.S.-Chinese relationship that have pushed the two countries toward more stability, and which make it more likely that the new diplomatic framework can survive. The current rapprochement is the fourth time in the past eight years that a period of tension between China and the United States has given way to an announcement of some kind of stable state. Ongoing friction has not derailed the consensus established in May. After China and the United States first aggressively confronted each other on trade and technology, culminating in the trade war in 2018, the two countries reached the Phase One trade agreement, in January 2020, which stabilized ties. The COVID-19 pandemic, which broke out soon afterward, severely inflamed tensions, sending the relationship to its lowest point since before U.S. President Richard Nixon first visited China, in 1972. In November 2022, Biden and Xi met in Bali and announced that they wanted to restabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, but just months later, in February 2023, recriminations over a Chinese object floating over the United States—described by Beijing as a civilian meteorological airship and by Washington as a spy balloon—interrupted such efforts. That November, Biden and Xi smoothed over ties for a third time at their San Francisco summit. This set the tenor of relations until April 2025, when Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs spawned a new trade war. Across this period, the United States went through three different presidential terms under both Democratic and Republican administrations, yet U.S.-Chinese relations repeatedly swung back to a stable state. Structural factors independent of any individual leader’s views encourage stability in the relationship. This includes the prohibitive cost of total economic decoupling and the catastrophic consequences of potential military conflict. Put differently, since the beginning of Trump’s second term, it has become clear to both sides that the bilateral relationship is simply too big to fail. The two sides occupy such important positions in global and international affairs, each with enough power to cause enormous damage, that neither wants to see the other become an enemy. The intense clashes between China and the United States over tariffs and rare earths in 2025 revealed that each side could exploit the other’s vulnerabilities, reminding them both that the two countries are highly interdependent and need to act prudently in an economic confrontation. Moreover, as nuclear powers, Beijing and Washington are aware that they cannot afford the prospect of a steadily deteriorating relationship that increases the risk of military conflict. If U.S.-Chinese relations again become more volatile after the next U.S. president takes office, it will test the resilience of the relationship. Yet the structural forces at play are unlikely to have changed. Even if future American leaders announce a new approach to the U.S.-Chinese relationship, therefore, in the end it is likely that they will come to the same realizations as their predecessors and seek stability. TANGLED UP IN RED Other critics argue that the consensus on strategic stability is, at most, a temporary truce. In their view, both sides will use this time to shore up their weaknesses, seek new sources of leverage, and prepare for a future confrontation. The United States could find alternate suppliers for the rare-earth elements it needs, for instance, and China could find new sources of semiconductors or develop its own advanced chips. But despite intense trade and geopolitical frictions, global supply chains have proved more resilient—and more deeply intertwined—than most observers anticipated. U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology have fragmented global supply chains, but they have not severed them. Attempts to route production away from China have merely dispersed Chinese enterprises across a wider array of countries and partners while retaining their irreplaceable role in most supply chains. In 2023, for instance, as the Biden administration sought to limit U.S. battery supply chains’ reliance on China, Chinese firms such as CATL actually expanded their market share by increasing production and supply networks in Asia and Europe, and CATL licensed its technology to Ford to produce batteries on U.S. soil. Even if China and the United States patch up their vulnerabilities in chips and rare earths, respectively, the two countries’ broader connections ensure that other areas of interdependence will remain. The rapid development of technologies such as artificial intelligence will make it particularly difficult for either the United States or China to eliminate the other’s sources of leverage. New technologies create new vulnerabilities. With the possibility of artificial general intelligence on the horizon, the frictions in the U.S.-Chinese relationship are unlikely to be concentrated in the same fields and to manifest themselves in the same ways as today. The likelihood of either China or the United States creating what Chinese martial arts novels call an “iron shirt”—a training regimen that makes someone impervious to blades and bullets—is very low. As both countries acquire more powerful, faster, and less predictable technological capabilities, what is needed to preserve stability is likely to change. Attempts by either side to achieve an overwhelming advantage or to ensure absolute security could instead heighten the other’s insecurity and intensify bilateral competition, ultimately forcing both countries to accept some mutual vulnerability and a different strategic equilibrium. The two countries are already realizing that they will have to manage the enormous challenges that AI presents, especially safety risks, whether through joint action or parallel efforts. U.S.-Chinese relations have stabilized four times over the past eight years; this also means that, viewed from the opposite perspective, the relationship has repeatedly devolved into confrontation. With each successive clash producing renewed grievances and hostility, a palpable fatigue has set in on both sides. Lowering their ambitions to the limited goal of stability makes it possible to dampen volatility, achieve tangible progress, and work with the reality of interdependence in more productive ways. THE EAST IS RISING One of the most significant changes underlying the acceptance of strategic stability is China’s growing confidence. When the first Trump administration began pushing for more decoupling, in 2018, many Chinese policymakers and citizens alike worried that escalating tensions with the United States would harm China’s progress and end the prospect of China developing into a stronger and wealthier country. In contemporary China, development is linked to openness: the more international cooperation there is, the faster technological development proceeds. The United States’ embrace of strategic competition challenged this basic premise. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which further drove countries apart and into blocs, made decision-makers and ordinary citizens worry even more. But after eight years of on-and-off trade and technology wars with the United States, China’s economic fundamentals have remained stable. Real estate markets are struggling and traditional industries are mired in distress, but high-tech industries have advanced by leaps and bounds and the manufacturing sector, particularly advanced manufacturing, has become stronger. China’s inability to obtain semiconductors from the United States has forced it to strengthen its own chip industry. The mainstream view in China now is that U.S. government restrictions on high-tech sectors have forced China onto a better path toward more self-reliance and innovation, rendering Washington’s containment policies ineffective and ultimately counterproductive. Structural factors have pushed the two countries toward more stability. China’s successes are mounting. In early 2025, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released a large language model that achieved near-parity with U.S. frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost. In April of that year, China successfully retaliated against Trump’s tariffs, forcing Washington back to the negotiating table. In those negotiations and later talks, China’s rare-earth dominance gave the country a chokepoint over U.S. supply chains. These episodes have increased China’s confidence and made its policymakers and strategists less worried about discussing competition as part of China’s relationship with the United States. Western commentators often believe that a confident China will become more assertive. The opposite is true. When China’s leaders believe that they can manage their external environment and that the country’s core interests and development prospects are not threatened, they are more willing to show restraint, engage in consultation, and focus on solving problems at home. In the 1990s and the first decade of the twenty-first century, for example, as China’s economy grew rapidly, it shelved disputes in the South China Sea with its neighbors. It was only after the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia,” when Beijing felt that the United States was uniting countries in the region against China, that it adopted a tougher approach to resolving disputes in the South China Sea. In 2026, a more confident China did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran, but instead quietly promoted peace talks behind the scenes. Likewise, now that China is less worried that the United States has either the intention or the ability to block China’s development prospects, it is more willing to accept a bounded competition with the United States. From a position of confidence, Beijing can engage the United States pragmatically on an issue-by-issue basis, looking to find specific policies to manage an inevitable amount of competition. A NEW BALLAST The fundamental requirement of the new framework of strategic stability is maintaining peace. That requires that the Chinese and U.S. militaries establish more mature measures for crisis avoidance, crisis management, and confidence building. The two sides can reduce the likelihood of conflict at low cost by setting up regularized military-to-military exchanges and fleshing out and expanding existing maritime and air encounter protocols. They can also coordinate on issues related to outer space, such as preventing near-earth-orbit collisions, regulating space traffic, and building trust around their respective strategic intentions. Addressing concerns in more politically sensitive domains, such as nuclear weapons and the military application of artificial intelligence, will require a more gradual approach. Although the Trump administration has shown heightened interest in discussing nuclear arms control with China, Beijing believes that formal negotiations are premature because of the vast disparity between U.S. and Chinese nuclear capabilities. Progress does not need to be confined to top leaders. More exchanges at all levels between China and the United States are another low-cost way of solidifying a framework of strategic stability. The United States and China could increase opportunities for engagement by easing visa restrictions and reviewing and reducing sanctions, removing entry or exit bans, and limiting other travel restrictions on institutions and citizens, as well as allowing more of the other side’s news media to operate there. Trump could take the opportunity to explicitly remind Chinese students that they are welcome to study in the United States, and Beijing could formulate clearer policies to guide scholars and students about the boundaries of acceptable research in China and guarantee openness, safety, and academic freedom for any scholarship falling outside those boundaries. Taiwan remains a dangerous flash point that could set back progress toward a relationship of strategic stability. Taiwan is the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict between China and the United States, and pressure is increasing. Continued rule of the island by the more pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, combined with Beijing’s strong desire to advance national unification and uncertainty about what kind of Taiwan policy the United States is going to pursue, has inflamed tensions on all sides. A new equilibrium can emerge only through an arrangement in which no party is completely satisfied yet each can live with the result. The goal is to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations. As long as Beijing believes that cross-strait integration remains achievable, it has no reason to resort to military force. The United States could shift its declared policy to align more closely with Beijing by recognizing Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan or by explicitly opposing Taiwan’s independence, which would reassure Beijing that the prospect of “peaceful reunification” remains viable. This would allow China and the United States to reach a consensus that realizes the U.S. objective of a peaceful resolution to the dispute yet also maintains the ability of the people in Taiwan to preserve their political and social systems. By keeping the prospect of peaceful reunification alive, the core concerns of all three parties can be accommodated as much as possible. Washington’s decision to pause $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, reached during Trump’s May summit with Xi, defused a rapidly escalating flash point in U.S.-Chinese relations. But it presents a new challenge to the nascent framework of strategic stability. Although Beijing certainly welcomed the delay, the pause has also raised expectations for future U.S. policy regarding Taiwan. Should the Trump administration eventually resume arms transfers—an outcome deemed likely by most Washington observers—Beijing will fiercely oppose the move, potentially jeopardizing the strategic stability framework. This scenario represents a concrete and salient threat that both countries must manage in the period ahead. A relationship of strategic stability is not a concept that one side imposed on the other or that will benefit Beijing but hurt Washington. It is the result of joint efforts by both countries, which makes it a rare opportunity. The next step is to build out this basic framework, breathe life into it, and make it sustainable. The September summit and additional scheduled leaders’ meetings this year offer a timely window of opportunity to make further small steps toward solidifying this baseline of stability. Some believe that this goal is too modest. But if two major powers such as China and the United States can keep fluctuations in the relationship within a manageable range and avoid any kind of war, it would be far more than a modest achievement. item.title: The Powder Keg in Outer Space
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.56
The United States, Russia, and China may not yet be in an arms race, but they are gearing up for one. Washington is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, strategic bomber, and ballistic missile submarine. Russia is developing a heavy ICBM and a new warhead while planning upgrades to its submarines and bombers. China has dug more than 300 new missile silos and fielded air-launched ballistic missiles, and it is developing a new generation of submarines and a stealth bomber. All three countries are making decisions about modernizing their nuclear weapons programs that will bear fruit in the decades to come—a notable reversal after decades in which the United States and Russia dismantled thousands of nuclear weapons and China seemed content maintaining a minimal deterrent. Yet it is in the space sector that the competition is intensifying most quickly. In the past decade, U.S. firms have pioneered highly capable small satellites, sent large constellations of them into orbit, and dramatically reduced launch costs. Russia has parked a satellite in an orbit that almost no other satellite uses, in a band of intense radiation more than 1,000 miles up, in what U.S. officials believe is a testing process for a nuclear antisatellite weapon that could one day take out satellite systems en masse. Russian satellites have sidled up to American and European spacecraft, and a Chinese satellite has towed a defunct spacecraft to a new orbit—maneuvers that demonstrate the ability to linger close enough to inspect another country’s satellite or, worse, eavesdrop on it, jam it, grab it, or disable it. Both Russia and China have tested missiles that destroy satellites; a Russian test in 2021 shattered an inactive satellite into more than a thousand pieces. The United States has demonstrated similar capabilities, though with less fanfare, and President Donald Trump has proposed placing thousands of antimissile interceptors in orbit as part of his Golden Dome project. Golden Dome aims to shield the entire United States from all missile threats launched from anywhere, including from Russia and China. This aspiration will shape the brewing arms competition more than anything else. Whether or not the so-called dome ever materializes, the decision to pursue this defensive buildup has likely already compelled Russian and Chinese planners to rethink their countries’ nuclear force structure. Given the long timelines of weapons development, they cannot risk doing otherwise. Both Moscow and Beijing will now plan for larger offensive forces—more missiles, more warheads per missile, more decoys, and more exotic delivery systems designed to fly under or around space-based interceptors—as well as weapons to attack the interceptors and sensors themselves. This will accelerate an arms race as each side fears losing its ability to retaliate, a fundamental requirement of nuclear stability. If the United States is to head off this dangerous cycle now, it needs to relearn a lesson that helped stabilize the U.S.-Soviet competition in the 1960s: arms control works only when countries agree to place limits on their defenses. GAME CHANGER Arms competition is a symptom of great-power enmity, but enmity alone does not induce an arms race. Powerful countries begin amassing arms when they grow concerned about a change in the strategic balance. The change that Russia and China have been responding to recently dates back to 2002, when U.S. President George W. Bush withdrew from the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty, paving the way for the United States to deploy a nationwide missile defense that Moscow and Beijing worried might one day be able to neutralize a retaliatory strike. Washington never created the system they feared. Today, the United States has only 44 ground-based interceptors—which have performed poorly in tests—to defend against intercontinental ballistic missiles. Although a few dozen interceptors is more than the zero the United States had in 2002, this number would be overwhelmed by even a small fraction of Russia’s roughly 1,500 deployed strategic warheads. But instead of responding to the system Washington actually built, Russia and China upgraded their offensive arsenals in response to the system they feared Washington might construct. When Russian President Vladimir Putin stood before his country’s legislature in March 2018 and unveiled a menagerie of exotic delivery systems—such as a nuclear-powered cruise missile, a nuclear-armed underwater drone, and a hypersonic boost-glide vehicle, all designed to evade U.S. defenses—he presented them as Russia’s answer to the U.S. withdrawal from the ABM Treaty 16 years earlier. China’s leaders also objected loudly to American missile defense plans, and over the past decade Beijing has sought to guarantee that it can overwhelm any U.S. defense by roughly doubling its nuclear stockpile and fielding an air-launched ballistic missile and a new submarine-launched missile to complete a triad. China has also practiced the launch of key strategic systems into the Pacific—in September 2024 it conducted its first full-range ICBM test in more than 40 years—and developed an orbital bombardment system that could evade U.S. radars and attack the United States. Both Russia and China have built and tested weapons that can threaten the satellites on which U.S. missile defenses depend. Enmity alone does not induce an arms race. There is always a lag between identifying an alarming shift in the strategic balance and developing a response to it. Budgets and bureaucracy can move at a glacial pace, and internal politics often determine the weapons and strategies a country pursues in surprising ways. In the 1970s, for instance, the Soviet Union developed a new generation of seemingly more accurate missiles, the SS-18 and SS-19—large, silo-based ICBMs that could each deliver multiple warheads to targets across the United States. The program was the outcome of a years-long bureaucratic battle in the late 1960s over how to respond to Washington’s development of the multiple-warhead Minuteman III missile. Chinese engineers, meanwhile, began exploring ways to counter U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s proposed missile defense system, the Strategic Defense Initiative, in the 1980s. But plans to improve China’s space-based capabilities languished for years until the 1999 U.S. bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade. The U.S. government said the attack was accidental—the target was a Yugoslav arms procurement agency—but the uproar loosened Chinese funding for various defense programs, including the development of an antisatellite weapon that Beijing finally tested in 2007 by smashing one of its own weather satellites in orbit. It’s too early to understand fully how internal politics are driving Russian and Chinese decisions about arms development today. Yet leaders in both Moscow and Beijing clearly see a need to respond to a U.S. defensive buildup. They may have overreacted after 2002, given the underwhelming nature of the missile defenses the United States has actually deployed and the efforts of U.S. officials across several administrations to reassure their Russian and Chinese counterparts that the purpose of those defenses was protection against North Korea and Iran, not to neutralize Russian or Chinese nuclear forces. But now, the Trump administration has explicitly embraced the goal of defending against “peer and near-peer adversaries”—a phrase that in Pentagon usage means Russia and China. This has surely made Moscow and Beijing believe that they were right all along. FICTION NO MORE The United States’ Golden Dome project will supercharge this competition. The space-based interceptors at the center of the U.S. proposal would attack Russian and Chinese missiles in their first minutes of flight, before they released their warheads and decoys, threatening to thin out the retaliatory strike that each country relies on to deter a U.S. attack. Russia and China will be seeking new missiles, warheads, and delivery systems that can breach those defenses. Even if there is some doubt about the viability of the Golden Dome, Russian and Chinese officials are obliged to take it seriously. When Reagan introduced the Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983, it was widely derided as “Star Wars”—science fiction. At the time, satellites were too large and launching them was too expensive to send an enormous cluster into orbit, as the project proposed. But today, SpaceX’s Starlink network, composed of thousands of relatively small satellites, demonstrates that very large constellations are feasible. Launching swarms of small, light interceptors to defend the United States from incoming nuclear missiles may no longer be so far-fetched. That is not to say the Golden Dome does not face problems. Missile defense systems have always struggled to be what analysts call “cost-effective at the margin.” An attacker can usually build and deploy a missile (or another warhead or a decoy) more cheaply than a defender can build and deploy enough interceptors to stop it. At the moment, the U.S. military plans to use four interceptors to target each warhead in space, and the kill vehicle—the technology that locates and collides with the warhead to destroy it—is particularly expensive. When North Korea paraded six mockup ICBMs in 2012, the United States responded by ordering 14 more interceptors. What those launchers and any missiles cost Pyongyang is unknown, but it was surely a tiny fraction of the roughly $1 billion Washington spent in response. Nor will the cost problem likely be solved with space-based interceptors. In theory, space-based interceptors might be cheaper than ground-based ones because an interceptor already in orbit does not need a large booster and can target a missile early, while it is moving slowly and easy to track. But even though satellite launches are getting cheaper, just a thin defense against the simplest targets will require thousands of satellite-based interceptors that must be continuously refreshed. A few thousand could easily turn into tens of thousands if the interceptors’ boosters do not accelerate quite as quickly, their sensors are not quite as sensitive, and communication with them is not quite as smooth as U.S. military planners anticipate, requiring a greater quantity to make up for shortcomings in quality. Relatively inexpensive efforts by Russia or China to increase their missile stocks or improve the effectiveness of their warheads would make it necessary for the United States to deploy even more interceptors. Starlink satellites may only cost a few hundred thousand to a million dollars, but they do not have an expensive kill vehicle built in. Those that have that capability are enormously expensive. The last space-based interceptor the United States designed—the Near Field Infrared Experiment, developed two decades ago—cost roughly $65 million per unit, adjusted for inflation. THE DANGER MOUNTS It is tempting to take comfort in the slow pace of an arms race. It is entirely possible that by the time these new systems are ready to be deployed, the conditions in which they might actually be used will have passed. Consider AUKUS, the 2021 agreement reached by Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States, to jointly produce a nuclear-powered submarine in response to China’s military buildup. When the first boat enters service in the early 2040s, a China led by a 90-year-old Xi Jinping—if he is even still alive—will be vastly different from the China of today. But slow is not the same as stable. The United States, Russia, and China are now all able to harass one another’s satellites in ways that have real consequences. Private companies would find it harder to operate commercial satellites if international cooperation on tracking space objects deteriorates amid this hostile maneuvering, and they would be on the hook for billions of dollars’ worth of assets that are not and will not be insured against acts of war or sabotage. All three countries are also locking themselves into decades-long force postures without knowing exactly what their adversaries’ forces will look like and despite the fact that space capabilities and frontier artificial intelligence models are advancing on much faster timelines. No one can really predict what technologies will be available in the early 2030s, when the U.S. Air Force hopes to deploy the first Sentinel ICBMs, which will replace the 1970s-era Minuteman III in 400 silos as the land-based leg of the U.S. nuclear deterrent. By then, Chinese missiles may be accurate and numerous enough to threaten those silos. AI-enabled reconnaissance could make mobile and concealed forces far easier to find. Or perhaps new space capabilities or AI-enabled cyberattacks will make space-based sensors, on which U.S. early warning depends, vulnerable in ways no one has anticipated. There is a risk that in their efforts to develop capabilities that threaten their adversaries’ space assets, one of the main players could wind up with a temporary incentive to strike first in a crisis—even if it would prefer not to strike at all. If Russia, for instance, places nuclear weapons in orbit, which it appears interested in doing, it might attempt to use those weapons to wipe out satellites to blind the United States at the outset of a conflict. China may similarly develop dangerous methods for destroying large numbers of satellites, including ground-launched “pop-up” boosters that could loft a nuclear warhead into space and detonate it before U.S. defenses could respond. Chinese military scientists have already published models of such a nuclear detonation. The blast would damage any unshielded satellites in line of sight and, as a 1962 U.S. test demonstrated, leave behind a belt of radiation that would continue killing satellites for months. Because this kind of mass attack in wartime would very likely degrade U.S. nuclear command-and-control systems, Washington would have to take seriously the prospect that such a strike in space could be the precursor to a nuclear strike on Earth. The mere possibility of losing its critical space assets in a surprise attack could push the United States to use its forces early or to delegate launch authority in ways that raise the risk of an accident, to avoid the devastating consequences. TIME TO TALK The fear that rapid technological advances could threaten nuclear stability is not new. U.S. and Soviet planners had the same concern in the 1960s, when missiles capable of carrying several warheads (known as multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles, or MIRVs), antiballistic missile systems, and antisatellite weapons became available all at once. The solution they chose was arms control. Arms control agreements aimed not only to reduce the number of nuclear weapons in U.S. and Soviet arsenals but also to provide a predictable basis for force planning. The effort met with mixed success. The 1972 SALT agreement limited the number of U.S. and Soviet missile launchers, and later treaties gradually reduced each side’s deployed strategic warheads from more than 10,000 then to 1,550 today. In the 1972 ABM Treaty, Washington and Moscow even managed to rein in some of the defensive deployments that can induce an adversary to develop its offensive capabilities—which is why the nuclear strategist Thomas Schelling, writing in Foreign Affairs four decades ago, identified that agreement as the “high point” of arms control. But negotiations stopped short of limiting MIRVs or antisatellite weapons, and arms control efforts stalled in the early 1980s; after Reagan unveiled his Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983, the project became the chief obstacle to reviving them. A renewed arms control effort can slow today’s arms race. The last remaining arms control agreement between Moscow and Washington, New START, lapsed in February, and for the first time since 1972, nothing limits Russia’s and the United States’ expansion of their offensive or defensive nuclear forces. Both countries—and China—are largely making decisions on the basis of fear and suspicion, not the joint pursuit of nuclear stability. Both Moscow and Beijing clearly see a need to respond to a U.S. defensive buildup. For now, U.S. plans for space make a comprehensive deal difficult to imagine. Moscow is at least conditionally open to one: Putin proposed in September 2025 that both sides informally observe New START’s limits for a year after it expired, and when Washington did not respond, Russia announced that it would hold to those limits only as long as the United States did. Beijing is less enthusiastic, but Chinese officials have been hinting at what they call a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” Writing on social media this year, Trump expressed interest in a “new, improved, and modernized Treaty that can last long into the future”—a treaty that administration officials have suggested might constrain all nuclear weapons, strategic and tactical, and include China as well as Russia. Yet the U.S. president is equally enthusiastic about the Golden Dome. Ultimately, these ambitions are in tension: Trump can have the treaty or the dome, but not both. Neither Moscow nor Beijing will limit their offensive forces or growing space capabilities without at least some predictability regarding the American defenses those forces are intended to defeat. Limiting offenses without also limiting defenses might allow the United States, in a crisis, to attempt a surprise attack on Russia or China and then rely on its powerful defenses to neutralize any surviving forces. This would leave Russia and China unable to retaliate and, as a result, vulnerable to coercion. The good news is that because most countries have a stake in expanding the commercial use of space, they have reason to try to reduce the dangers in that domain alongside efforts to negotiate a new treaty to limit strategic arms. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, to which the United States, Russia, and China are all parties, already bans placing nuclear weapons in space. It lacks verification, but this problem could be addressed if the signatories agreed to inspections of payloads either before launch or, in extraordinary cases, while in orbit. Every country with satellites in orbit should support a ban on antisatellite weapon tests that result in debris and pursue cooperation on space traffic control to reduce the risk of collisions. All of this becomes more feasible with some defensive limits in place. The idea of restricting defenses against nuclear attack has long been a third rail in American politics, especially among Republicans. But many former Republican orthodoxies have proved negotiable; the party staunchly supported free trade and NATO, and opposed Russia just as strongly, until Trump decided otherwise. An agreement, moreover, does not have to eliminate defenses entirely. The ABM Treaty allowed each party to maintain two missile defense sites, later reduced to one. What a new deal needs to do is to place verifiable limits on defenses that give the other parties a sense of predictability. Without such limits, the United States, Russia, and China are likely to continue expanding their offensive forces, developing ever more exotic delivery systems, and pursuing new ways to attack each other’s satellites. All three will blame their adversaries for making the buildup necessary, but in truth each country will be racing itself, driven by its own fears and internecine politics. It’s hard to imagine how anyone wins such a race—other than by not running at all.
