item.title: A Great Rebalancing Is Coming
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.40
The trade imbalances that have come to characterize the global economy are fundamentally untenable. China, Germany, and a handful of other economies run large, persistent trade surpluses, while the United States absorbs much of these surpluses by running the world’s largest trade deficit. Sooner or later, something must give. For an advanced, capital-rich economy such as that of the United States, an enduring trade deficit will bring with it either rising unemployment or rising debt, neither of which is sustainable. In theory, the major surplus and deficit economies could agree on a coordinated adjustment in which surplus countries would expand domestic demand and deficit countries would gradually reduce their dependence on debt-fueled consumption, allowing the imbalances to shrink without a sharp contraction in global demand. That would be the sensible solution. But because the major players disagree about the causes of the imbalances, they are unlikely to come to such a solution. China attributes them to excessive U.S. consumption and fiscal deficits; the United States blames foreign industrial, trade, and currency policies; and Europe has yet to settle on a coherent diagnosis. As a result, they all have proposed remedies that are at odds with one another. Beijing wants deficit countries to save more and prefers not to change China’s growth model. Washington wants surplus countries to reduce their surpluses by redistributing income to the household sector. European leaders continue to advocate for multilateral cooperation and rules-based trade. This makes the chances of a coordinated response slim. And as the economic analyst Martin Wolf wrote in the Financial Times earlier this year, if there is little prospect of preemptive action, “the second-best option is to prepare for a crisis.” Individual economies are now doing just that. History shows that trade imbalances of this scale almost always end painfully—and that the pain of the adjustment is not distributed evenly. High levels of debt combined with low productivity makes a country more likely to bear the burden of a trade adjustment, but economic and political power can also give it the tools to pass the burden off to others. Among the three main economic players today, China is the most vulnerable, the United States has the most capacity to reduce its exposure, and Europe possesses latent power but a dubious ability to use it. None of their maneuvers to protect themselves are likely to reduce the risk or overall cost of a crisis. The question is only who will feel the brunt of the losses when it arrives. HISTORY REPEATS ITSELF Large, persistent trade imbalances have cropped up periodically over the past century, and they are rarely benign. One such episode occurred during the 1920s, when a surge in American productivity was not accompanied by rising wages. Production soared past consumption, and the United States ran enormous trade surpluses. Europe ran the corresponding deficits, as many countries borrowed heavily abroad to rebuild economies devastated by war. Germany in particular borrowed extensively to finance both domestic growth and its reparations payments. American domestic debt also rose rapidly, much of it to fund consumption and asset speculation. As the imbalances persisted and U.S. manufacturing expanded at the expense of European manufacturing, protectionist pressures intensified. France devalued its currency in 1927, the United Kingdom abandoned the gold standard in 1931, and the same year Germany imposed import restrictions and rationed access to foreign currency. Even the United States, whose manufacturers and farmers complained that weak demand was threatening domestic production and employment, passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act in 1930. The adjustment came in the form of a collapse in global trade during the Great Depression of the early and mid-1930s. Nearly every major economy suffered from the contraction, but they did not suffer equally. Those with large deficits, such as the United Kingdom, recovered more quickly and suffered less severe financial distress than the United States, which absorbed a disproportionate share of the costs. American exports fell faster than imports, domestic investment imploded, banks failed, and bankruptcies surged. Trade imbalances on a large scale almost always end painfully. The next major episode of persistent trade imbalances was the rare case in which the imbalances faded away without causing major disruption. During the 1950s and 1960s, the United States again ran very large surpluses while Europe and Japan ran corresponding deficits. Similar to the situation in the 1920s, these deficits financed the reconstruction of postwar economies as resources poured into infrastructure and manufacturing. But unlike in the earlier period, governments maintained strict controls over capital flows and imported capital mostly to fund investments that generated enough future income to service the associated liabilities. Because the investments were so productive, debt rose little relative to GDP. There was also minimal protectionist pressure, largely because Europe and Japan urgently needed imports and the United States actively encouraged reconstruction in both places. As a result of these unusual conditions, trade imbalances disappeared gradually without any countries bearing severe costs. Four more episodes of trade imbalances would follow, all of them ending in pain for the countries involved. One happened in Latin America during the 1970s. The oil shocks of that period, in which the global price of oil soared from roughly $2 per barrel at the beginning of the decade to around $30 per barrel by the end, generated massive petrodollar surpluses in the oil-exporting economies of the Middle East and other members of OPEC. Much of this was deposited in major international banks that, eager to find new customers, loaned the funds to Latin American and other developing economies, eventually leading to overvalued currencies and large trade deficits. By the early 1980s, rising global interest rates made their debt unsustainable. Debt crises resolved the trade imbalances but left the deficit countries with the overwhelming share of the adjustment costs: recession, inflation, austerity, and lost decades of growth. The next case developed during the late 1970s and 1980s. Japanese productivity growth outpaced Japanese wages during this period, and the country began running enormous trade surpluses. The same happened in Germany, allowing the country’s manufacturing sector to become increasingly competitive internationally. The United Kingdom and the United States ran deficits that accommodated both Japan’s and Germany’s surpluses. Japan in particular saw a spectacular surge in domestic debt during the 1980s, as extremely high levels of investment flowed into projects whose returns fell far below expectations. China has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can. Protectionist pressures rose steadily, culminating in the Plaza Accord of 1985, in which the world’s major economies agreed to appreciate the yen and the deutsche mark against the dollar in an effort to reduce trade imbalances. Yet a real resolution of the imbalances did not come until Japan’s economic downturn in the 1990s, which brought collapsing asset prices, persistent deflation, and years of stagnation. It is difficult to compare this to Germany’s experience, however, given that the 1990 unification of East and West Germany fundamentally altered the economy at precisely the same time. The Asian financial crisis of the 1990s in some ways resembled the Latin American trade imbalances of the 1970s. In the early part of the decade, foreign capital poured into a group of East Asian economies. These economies developed large trade deficits, which were balanced by surpluses in Japan, European countries, and, increasingly, China. Although their domestic and external debt rose rapidly, protectionism remained limited. Even so, when investor confidence broke in 1997, the adjustment was swift and brutal. Currency collapses, banking crises, and deep recessions struck the East Asian deficit countries, while the surplus countries bore few costs. Finally, between roughly 2002 and 2008, Germany accumulated large surpluses after implementing labor reforms that pushed wage growth down relative to productivity growth and caused huge increases in saving. It exported more and more to Greece, Portugal, Spain, and several other eurozone economies, which in turn accumulated deficits financed by rapidly rising debt. Because this dynamic emerged within the eurozone, where most members shared a common currency, countries could not impose protectionist measures and exchange-rate adjustment was impossible. When the 2008 global financial crisis triggered the eurozone crisis, the deficit countries experienced sovereign debt crises, unemployment, austerity, and prolonged stagnation that unwound the imbalances. COST ANALYSIS These events demonstrate that trade imbalances become dangerous when they are accompanied by rapidly rising debt and growing financial fragility in either surplus or deficit economies. If a country with a surplus uses its high savings to finance productive investment at home or abroad, the imbalance can persist for many years without causing serious economic disruption. But if instead its excess savings finance unproductive investment at home or drive high household consumption, asset bubbles, or persistent fiscal deficits in the economies of its trading partners, the whole system becomes increasingly shaky. Protectionism is generally not the cause of trade conflicts, but rather a symptom of imbalances that have endured for too long. Its absence does not make the eventual adjustment less painful. Yet when countries adopt protectionist policies, they can influence where the adjustment occurs and who bears the costs. Whether it is surplus or deficit economies that take on those costs may also depend on which side has the greater ability to use trade, financial, or exchange-rate policies to compel the other to adjust. Deficit countries more often bear the costs when they are politically weak and unable to finance themselves independently, defend their currencies, or restrict capital and trade flows without triggering a financial crisis—as Latin American countries were in the early 1980s, much of East Asia was in 1997, and southern Europe was after 2008. Surplus countries are at risk, meanwhile, when deficit countries have sufficiently strong economies and political systems to reduce their own deficits by restricting imports, limiting capital inflows, depreciating their currencies, or otherwise preventing the surplus countries from exporting their excess savings. This is what happened to the United States in the early 1930s and to Japan beginning in the 1990s. Their trade partners reduced their deficits by intervening to reduce imports and increase exports, forcing the U.S. and Japanese surplus-based growth models to unravel as investment collapsed and exports, profits, and asset prices fell. The main takeaway for governments today is twofold. First, the place where debt has risen furthest without a corresponding rise in productive capacity is most at risk when an adjustment to a trade imbalance eventually arrives. Second, the countries involved in imbalanced trade can take action to push adjustment costs onto others, but their success depends largely on economic power and their ability to wield it. THE CRISIS TO COME Today’s global trade imbalances are unusually large, and the coming adjustment is likely to be especially difficult. China looks most vulnerable. Its debt burden is already among the world’s highest; the country has experienced perhaps the fastest increase in debt relative to GDP in history. Much of this debt has funded investment that has generated progressively lower—even negative—economic returns, including excess residential real estate, underutilized infrastructure, and manufacturing capacity that far outstrips demand. This huge and growing debt burden creates enormous pressure on Beijing to take any steps necessary to avoid absorbing the bulk of the adjustment costs. China will almost certainly try to push as much of this burden as possible onto its trade partners. It has every incentive to maintain the largest possible trade surplus for as long as it can, allowing excess production to be absorbed abroad rather than forcing a sharp contraction in domestic production and employment. In doing so, China can spread the adjustment over many years as it gradually works down its debt, while its trading partners endure greater costs in the form of larger trade deficits, rising debt, deindustrialization, or weaker growth. If foreign protectionist measures or weaker external demand make this strategy impossible, however, China’s economy would face some combination of slower growth, rising unemployment, falling investment, and financial distress. Whether Beijing can offload the costs of adjustment depends on the willingness of the rest of the world to absorb them. Washington has little reason to continue allowing large, persistent trade deficits. As the world’s largest economy and by far its largest source of demand, the United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit and stop acting as the world’s consumer of last resort. And because U.S. trade policy is centralized within the executive branch—with the president able to impose tariffs, investment restrictions, and export controls under broad statutory authority—Washington has the political ability to exercise this power. If the United States uses industrial policy to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and, more important, takes greater control over its trade and capital flows using tariffs and other restrictive measures, China and other major surplus economies will not be able to maintain their surpluses with corresponding U.S. deficits. They will have to either reduce those surpluses with a painful contraction in domestic production or find new importers among countries that remain both willing and able to absorb them. The United States has the economic power to reduce its deficit. This leaves Europe in perhaps the most difficult position. The eurozone is the world’s third-largest economy and its second-largest source of demand, so Europe has economic power at its disposal. What is much less clear is whether it has the political ability to exercise this power, given its fragmented policymaking institutions and the often divergent interests of its member states. If the United States is able to reduce its trade deficit and expand its share of global manufacturing while China resists an equivalent contraction in its surpluses, a politically divided Europe could be forced to take on larger deficits almost by default. The costs could include deindustrialization, rising debt, and weaker growth. This process may have begun already. Once the major economies stop asking how to minimize the global costs of adjustment and begin asking instead how to minimize their own risk, the opportunity to find a relatively painless solution to the global trade imbalance will have passed. Beijing seems set on trying to preserve its surpluses for as long as possible. Washington is just as intent on reducing its deficits. If Europe can develop the political capacity to do the same, the burden of adjustment will increasingly fall onto the surplus economies, which would have to rely more on domestic demand and less on exports. If it cannot, Europe will absorb more and more of the global surpluses, and what appears today to be a trade conflict mainly between China and the United States may become a conflict between China and Europe—and a struggle between the two of them to avoid bearing steeper costs down the road. History makes clear that trade imbalances are always resolved eventually. What remains uncertain is how damaging the resolution will be—and for whom. item.title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.20
Separated from China by a roughly 100-mile-wide strait, Taiwan relies on its navy as the first line of defense against a potential invasion. It must be able to prevent an assault by a Chinese force carried across the Taiwan Strait in large amphibious ships. Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet, both as visible symbols of state power and as tools for signaling resolve in the face of Chinese coercion, and Taiwan’s current shipbuilding plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large and expensive new ships. Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack. China has invested in cutting-edge intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (collectively known as ISR), as well as electronic warfare systems, drones, and missiles. Taiwan’s large surface ships are now a liability. But Taiwan has an advantage: these same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives. Taipei can take advantage of this mismatch by replacing its destroyers and frigates with a greater number of smaller surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial wave of Chinese strikes and remain capable of attacking a Chinese invasion fleet. The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates. These large ships are impediments to the radical transformation of the Taiwanese navy that the Chinese threat requires. Building ships of this size with stealth features and defense systems to survive a battle in the Taiwan Strait would be prohibitively costly; without these features, they would be too vulnerable to play a major role in the navy’s primary wartime mission of denying a Chinese invasion force the use of the Taiwan Strait. Efforts elsewhere to build similarly capable ships have proved costly and difficult. The U.S. Navy’s Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capabilities needed to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters. In comparison, the spending on Taiwan’s entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually. Rather than spend resources on large ships, Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait. Combined with current plans to build shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with antiship missiles, and eight submarines, Taiwan can create a dispersed and hard-to-destroy defense system that can withstand Chinese attacks and repel a potential amphibious assault. SITTING DUCKS Large ships may be potent signals of national power, but they are relatively easy to target and politically costly to lose. When ships are fighting in narrow waterways under heavy surveillance, visibility quickly becomes a deadly liability. The sinking of a large ship can also have consequences beyond an immediate military setback. A highly visible and costly loss may make political and military leaders more cautious about risking additional warships as conflict continues. Major naval engagements over more than the last four decades suggest that any navy expecting to fight near an enemy’s coast should be wary of building its force structure around expensive, irreplaceable hulls. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, for example, showed how a single successful strike on a warship can constrain an entire surface fleet. Argentina entered the Falklands conflict with powerful ships, including the cruiser General Belgrano and the aircraft carrier Veinticinco de Mayo. But after a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war. In the Persian Gulf six years later, the U.S. Navy’s ability to combine surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons devastated Iranian naval forces during Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates. Whereas the Falklands War illustrated the political consequences of losing a major warship, Praying Mantis highlighted the danger for ships facing an adversary with a much more effective “kill chain”—the sensors and communications to detect, identify, track, target, and attack an opponent’s fleet. For Taiwan, the lesson is that the combat power of large warships is irrelevant if they cannot survive long enough to fight, and an early loss could have cascading effects on the navy’s sustained combat operations. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. Losing a smaller ship is less costly politically and militarily than losing a larger warship. In 2006, for instance, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit, which was operating in the waters off Lebanon. The ship had not been warned of the threat and had little time to detect and respond to a missile launched from shore 12 miles away, and some of its defensive systems were not fully activated. The missile killed four sailors and damaged the ship’s equipment, but the crew contained the damage and the Hanit limped home. The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes. Most important for Taiwan, Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign after Russia’s invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet. The campaign combined land-based antiship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones, and external intelligence to impose heavy costs on Russian naval operations in the Black Sea. These attacks helped push much of Russia’s fleet farther from Ukraine’s shores. The sinking of the flagship Moskva, for example, showed that even a ship equipped with layered air defenses was vulnerable to an adversary’s kill chain. The ongoing war in Iran reinforces this pattern: the United States and Israel severely damaged Iran’s surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats. The result is that Iran, despite losing much of its conventional naval power, has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz. SMALL IS BEAUTIFUL As these examples show, a less powerful navy does not need to control its coastal waters to deny a stronger adversary the ability to use them. In the Taiwan Strait, therefore, the goal should be “sea denial”: preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion. Achieving sea denial does not require Taiwan to abandon its surface navy. But it must build a different kind of fleet—one based on a greater number of smaller ships that can operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks, making the fleet more likely to survive an initial assault and repel an invasion force. Finland and Sweden are good models. Both countries must deter and defend against a larger, more powerful adversary—Russia—and they are simultaneously contesting sovereignty challenges to areas they control and preparing for potential amphibious attacks on their coasts. With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas. They have escorted away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodged diplomatic protests with Moscow. Both countries have extensive, sophisticated, and steadily improving surveillance, communications, and decision-support networks. A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. In July, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te attended the commissioning ceremony of the navy’s eighth and newest missile patrol ship—a lightweight but heavily armed corvette built in Taiwan with an innovative catamaran hull that makes the ship faster and more stable—and four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan’s shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become. Sustained production would bring costs down, and each successive batch of vessels can incorporate new weapons, sensors, and uncrewed systems as they develop. Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion. These changes should be combined with a broader upgrading of Taiwan’s armed forces’ network of sensors, communications tools, drones, and missiles. Taiwan is already making some of these investments. Its most recent special budget and the next round of its naval plans strengthen the kill chain with maritime surveillance drones, upgraded command-and-control networks to direct and coordinate military forces, and artificial intelligence–assisted combat decision support systems. These are the essential building blocks of an effective system to deny China the ability to freely navigate the Taiwan Strait. But the same technologies that make Taiwan’s kill chain more effective also make its large surface ships susceptible to attacks. Only by restructuring and upgrading its surface fleet can Taiwan be ready for a potential invasion. A restructured Taiwanese surface fleet would also support plans to build eight new submarines, the first of which is already in sea trials. Submarines are slower but stealthier than corvettes. Missiles and drones launched from corvettes can disable ships by hitting them above the surface, and torpedoes launched from submarines can sink them. Changing its approach to its surface fleet is a key part of how Taiwan can make its other naval investments more effective. RIGHTING THE SHIP The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical. Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement, and visible proof of the government’s commitment to national security. By contrast, the public cannot see a warehouse full of drones or a mobile missile launcher hidden in the mountains. For navy leadership, too, the status quo is easier than pushing for major change. Taiwan’s destroyers and frigates, many of which are based on 50-year-old American designs, are well understood and therefore institutionally safe choices. But rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs. Moving away from familiar platforms will require political and military leaders to take risks and overcome the setbacks and criticism that accompany any institutional change. Production of Taiwan’s first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule. But such challenges are inevitable when dealing with complex vessels and should not derail necessary investments. Government and defense leaders need to sustain support for these programs and justify their importance to the public, even when opposition politicians criticize them. After years of stagnation and decline, Taiwan’s defense spending is finally increasing. Taiwan’s proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May (a significant sum, albeit down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch). But Taiwan will not be more secure if these resources are spent on outdated defense concepts and a small number of vulnerable large warships. The country needs a dispersed, agile, and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait. Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion. item.title: What Makes a Good Counterterrorism Strategy?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.36
What Makes a Good Counterterrorism Strategy? Three top experts on the terror threat 25 years after 9/11. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. Here’s what’s on tap for the day: The counterterrorism landscape 25 years after 9/11, Germany’s reluctance to punish Russia more severely, and the United States and Iran continuing to exchange fire. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. Here’s what’s on tap for the day: The counterterrorism landscape 25 years after 9/11, Germany’s reluctance to punish Russia more severely, and the United States and Iran continuing to exchange fire. Avoiding Whiplash Twenty-five years after the 9/11 attacks, global jihadism is no longer viewed as the top terrorism threat to the U.S. homeland, and Washington’s foreign-policy priorities have shifted away from counterterrorism and toward great-power competition. But terrorism remains a challenge for the United States both at home and abroad, particularly as its adversaries increasingly look to exploit rapidly evolving technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI). At the Soufan Center’s Global Summit on Terrorism and Political Violence in New York City on Wednesday, John moderated a fireside chat with three top experts—who served and advised both Republican and Democratic administrations—on what a 21st-century counterterrorism strategy should look like. Much of the discussion focused on how Washington can best confront emerging threats. The 9/11 Commission Report attributed the attacks, in part, to a “failure of imagination” from the U.S. government and intelligence community. Asked whether the United States is currently failing to imagine new terror threats to the homeland, Jen Easterly, who served as the director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency from 2021 to 2025, recalled how the Boston Marathon bombers learned how to make explosives via a digital al Qaeda magazine—and related this to the capabilities that AI offers. For instance, she said, imagine AI generating instructions, precision imagery, or even shopping lists for “crude versions” of cyber, biological, and radiological weapons and putting that at the hands of hostile nations, terrorists, and criminals. This is “the world that we are racing toward at world-class marathon speed,” said Easterly, who is now the CEO of RSAC, a leading cybersecurity conference. There have already been examples of jihadi groups, including Boko Haram, using AI to help with a range of activities, from producing propaganda to planning attacks. Partnerships and learning. AI is far from the only technology that’s exposing counterterrorism vulnerabilities for the United States and its allies. Drones and cyberattacks are also major concerns, particularly in relation to state-sponsored terrorism amid the Russia-Ukraine and U.S.-Iran wars. Maintaining and cultivating strong international partnerships will be crucial to confronting such challenges, the experts said. The United States can better understand the threats that it’s facing by communicating with international partners that have faced similar threats, said Chris Costa, who served as a special assistant to the president and senior director for counterterrorism at the National Security Council during the first Trump administration. “We have to share those lessons,” Costa said. “Our adversaries are absolutely learning creatures,” he added. “They are learning day in and day out. We have to continue to learn as well.” With the Trump administration’s penchant for antagonizing allies via insulting rhetoric (or provocative maps), tariffs, and other policies, there are fair questions to ask about the potential long-term consequences for U.S. intelligence gathering and counterterrorism. The White House’s counterterrorism strategy has also generated controversy, with its focus on going after “narcoterrorists” and left-wing groups (and no attention granted to threats posed by the far right). Experts have said that the strategy is at odds with reality and driven by ideology. In the discussion at the summit on Wednesday, the experts emphasized the importance of having an intelligence-driven, non-partisan counterterrorism strategy. Though Costa declined to directly criticize the Trump administration, he said that building “trust” with foreign partners requires having a counterterrorism strategy that is “based on facts, based on the intelligence.” When asked whether the United States is being complacent in confronting jihadism as it increasingly focuses on other threats, Joshua Geltzer, who served as a deputy assistant to the president, deputy White House counsel, and legal advisor to the National Security Council under the Biden administration, said the “diffuseness of the terrorism threat … justifies speaking about a range of threats,” but that “jihadism’s still among them.” “Whiplash is a really bad way to do most things, but especially counterterrorism,” Geltzer added. “Unfortunately, the adversary gets a vote. We need our resources to be well allocated.” On the Button What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already. Iran war escalates (again). Iran and the United States continued exchanging tit-for-tat strikes near the Strait of Hormuz this week, with Iran claiming that it had targeted 10 ships and fired missiles at a U.S. military base in Jordan, a day after U.S. Central Command said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers. The Wall Street Journal also reported that Iran has begun producing ballistic missiles again, citing U.S. and Middle Eastern officials. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, meanwhile, seized a key port in the Red Sea, potentially giving the Iranian regime control of a second shipping chokepoint in the region’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Berlin’s Russia problem. Germany recently accused Russia of being behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport. Berlin has taken a number of steps to punish Moscow, which has denied involvement, but some critics feel that its actions are far too tepid and won’t deter future acts of hybrid warfare or what some are calling “state-sponsored terrorism.” John and Sam Skove wrote about these developments, and how domestic political concerns are influencing Germany’s approach to this, in a new piece this week. Snapshot Hot Mic The FBI on Wednesday became the latest U.S. agency to release a cyber strategy, and it did so in an unclassified manner for the first time in the bureau’s history. The 17-page document expands on the Trump administration’s broader cyber doctrine, which advocates more offensive cyberattacks against U.S. adversaries—including in partnership with private companies. The FBI strategy “will direct all 56 field offices on how to pursue counter cyber efforts on behalf of the American people,” Brett Leatherman, the assistant director of the FBI’s cyber division, told reporters on the sidelines of a cybersecurity conference in Washington shortly after announcing the strategy onstage. That includes joint operations with companies such as CrowdStrike and Microsoft, which are frequently targeted by nation-state hackers themselves. Asked by SitRep about fears that this would open up those companies to retaliation, Leatherman said that foreign nations “are using industry right now to hack us in ways that are outside the norms of cyberspace operations.” But, he said, the United States has “to do it in a way that is lawful. We have to do it in a way that protects organizations just like you protect our own personnel.” Leatherman also told SitRep that which companies the FBI works with will depend in part on which systems are being targeted and who is best positioned to address a particular hack. “It’s opportunistic based on what the actors are doing in those environments and what capabilities the industry partners bring to that,” he said. Put on Your Radar Saturday, Sept. 12: The two-day BRICS summit begins in India. U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit Ireland. Sunday, Sept. 13: Sweden holds parliamentary elections. The European Union hosts a two-day Arctic summit. Monday, Sept. 14: The International Atomic Energy Agency general conference begins. Wednesday, Sept. 16: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her State of the European Union address. Thursday, Sept. 17: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addresses the European Parliament. By the Numbers 37—The percentage of Americans who say the United States is unlikely to elect a woman president in their lifetime, according to a new survey from the Pew Research Center. That figure is up from 26 percent in 2023. Quote of the Week “This is actual coercion, bullying, and aggression.” —Philippine National Secretary of Defense Gilberto C. Teodoro Jr., holding up a note that he claimed China passed him onstage at a defense forum in South Korea that criticized a 2016 legal ruling on Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea by an independent tribunal in The Hague. FP’s Most Read This Week - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Welcome to the New Defense-Dominant World by Stephen M. Walt Whiskey Tango Foxtrot Trump used his speech at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday to pledge $5,000 to every adult American if the Republicans win the November midterm election and retain control of the House and Senate. “It will be called the Trump dividend,” the U.S. president said. As many have pointed out, keeping that promise would cost $1 trillion and, as it stands, would likely be illegal. Correction, Sept. 10, 2026: This newsletter has been updated to correct a quote. item.title: The ‘Super-Terrorist’ We Still Can’t Escape
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.07
The ‘Super-Terrorist’ We Still Can’t Escape Carlos the Jackal left behind a violent, celebrity-obsessed world. When I first entered the counterterrorism world in 1997 as an attorney at the U.S. Department of Justice, a sea change was underway in the field. Historically, terrorists were animated by the desire, in expert Brian Jenkins’ words, to have “a lot of people watching, not a lot of people dead.” In the latter half of the 20th century, hijackings rarely resulted in mass casualties; there were targeted assassinations and horrific killings—the 1972 Munich Olympics come to mind—but, at least in the terrorists’ minds, they were carried out for a specific goal, such as Palestinian statehood. The most famous of these old-school terrorists was Carlos the Jackal, the Venezuelan-born killer who became the improbable face of Palestinian resistance and whose reign of terror captivated the world throughout the 1970s. But by 2000, when I was serving on the National Commission on Terrorism, a bipartisan congressional panel tracking the looming threat of al Qaeda, we were warning of a different mindset, one that would come to rattle U.S. domestic security: Terrorists now wanted a lot of people dead and a lot of people watching. A new mastermind, Osama bin Laden, had replaced Carlos as the global icon of terrorism. The 9/11 attacks that he orchestrated the following year would go on to transform U.S. homeland security, domestic surveillance, and the nature of global terrorism beyond recognition. When I first entered the counterterrorism world in 1997 as an attorney at the U.S. Department of Justice, a sea change was underway in the field. Historically, terrorists were animated by the desire, in expert Brian Jenkins’ words, to have “a lot of people watching, not a lot of people dead.” In the latter half of the 20th century, hijackings rarely resulted in mass casualties; there were targeted assassinations and horrific killings—the 1972 Munich Olympics come to mind—but, at least in the terrorists’ minds, they were carried out for a specific goal, such as Palestinian statehood. The most famous of these old-school terrorists was Carlos the Jackal, the Venezuelan-born killer who became the improbable face of Palestinian resistance and whose reign of terror captivated the world throughout the 1970s. But by 2000, when I was serving on the National Commission on Terrorism, a bipartisan congressional panel tracking the looming threat of al Qaeda, we were warning of a different mindset, one that would come to rattle U.S. domestic security: Terrorists now wanted a lot of people dead and a lot of people watching. A new mastermind, Osama bin Laden, had replaced Carlos as the global icon of terrorism. The 9/11 attacks that he orchestrated the following year would go on to transform U.S. homeland security, domestic surveillance, and the nature of global terrorism beyond recognition. Joby Warrick’s new book, The Jackal: The Rise and Fall of Carlos, the World’s First Super-Terrorist, has been released at the very moment when Americans will be reflecting on bin Laden and what these 25 years have wrought. Although Carlos may not at first seem to be relevant to the post-9/11 world, this account of his life forces us to reconsider. Warrick, a veteran Washington Post reporter, not only offers a detailed and engaging prelude to the era that bred bin Laden but also reminds us how Carlos’s legacy still resonates in the performative tactics of so many terrorist threats today. By the time we finally meet Carlos, whose real name is Ilich Ramírez Sánchez, Warrick has teased his interview with the infamous killer for most of the book. The moment itself is masterfully told: Instead of a formidable figure or sinister criminal, the Carlos that Warrick encounters is not particularly interesting. He’s a man in his 70s who is spending the rest of his life in a French jail, boasting to Warrick that he “should have killed a few more people.” He reminisces of the good old times, when he was famous and lethal, and still harbors resentment toward those who betrayed him and facilitated his capture. Most of all, he seems worried that he will be forgotten. This is not the man the world witnessed decades ago. For those who missed the Jackal’s reign of terror, there was nothing quite like it. Between 1973 and 1985, he was effectively a celebrity terrorist, a man who garnered global rock star status with his carefully manicured image, known for his black beret and dark sunglasses. Journalists profiled him extensively. As Warrick wrote, “Carlos intuitively understood [that] fame has its own intrinsic weight” and would “ride his fame like a rocket.” “I am the famous Carlos! You know who I am,” he told the huddling group of OPEC negotiators during an audacious kidnapping at a 1975 conference in Vienna. By then, they almost certainly did. The name we know Sánchez by is reflective of his cultivated persona. “Carlos” was simply the nickname a terror cell recruiting officer gave him. But I had always assumed that The Day of the Jackal, Frederick Forsyth’s 1971 novel about a professional assassin who attempts to kill the French president, was based on Carlos. It turns out that one of many tabloids that covered Carlos referred to him as “the Jackal” after a copy of the novel was found at his safehouse in London. Carlos adopted it as his own because it was good branding. Carlos may have turned to the Palestinian cause for a similar reason. Aside from his Marxist father, there was little in his upbringing that would naturally tie him to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP). He seemed to find the resistance group as an escape hatch after his expulsion from college. But once accepted into the group, his audacity, boldness, and charm catapulted him into the senior leadership. He planned and executed the 1973 assassination attempt on Jewish businessman Joseph Sieff in London, a 1974 grenade attack in Paris, and the 1975 rocket attacks on El Al planes at France’s Orly Airport. After Sieff survived and the El Al planes were not destroyed, Carlos needed a win. By the end of 1975, he led the audacious OPEC raid that resulted in three dead and around 60 hostages flown to Algeria and Libya. His philosophy, if he had one at all, was always somewhat muddled. As Warrick recounts, Carlos purported to hate the West and its excesses in theory, but loved its hotels, cars, and jewelry. He eventually became a convert, but for much of his life he was not much of an adherent to Islam. He was fond of partying, alcohol, and women. He was fearless about killing—French authorities wanted him for the death of over a dozen French citizens, including multiple counterintelligence officers—but he was also frequently not very good at it: He led a lot of missions that were aborted or botched, and he was overly confident in his planning and in his belief that leaders such as Libya’s Muammar al-Qaddafi, who armed the OPEC attack but turned on Carlos when he sought refuge, were reliable. By 1979, Carlos was reduced to a man for hire by those who wanted him to knock off competitors or individuals who slighted them. Among his most notorious clients was Romania’s communist dictator, Nicolae Ceausescu, who hired Carlos to assassinate Romanian dissidents throughout Europe and bomb Radio Free Europe’s Romanian broadcast studio in Munich. Warrick’s sweeping and engaging biography of Carlos is as much a history of the man as it is of the era. Carlos’s travels take the reader from Baghdad to Beirut to Belgrade and serve as a window into major flashpoints in the Middle East. Qaddafi, Palestine Liberation Organization chairman Yasar Arafat, and Iraqi President Saddam Hussein all play prominent roles. Even a young bin Laden makes a cameo appearance. In the mid-1970s, Carlos had briefly targeted the wealthy bin Laden family, surveilling them while they were on vacation in Lebanon’s Chouf mountains as potential kidnapping victims who could be held for a large ransom. Carlos followed the family to a resort but eventually abandoned the effort to focus on the PFLP’s OPEC attack. A reader is hard-pressed not to wonder about the trajectory of history had such a kidnapping occurred. Shortly after the OPEC raid, Carlos’s mentor, Wadi Haddad, banished him from the PFLP for disobeying orders. In the years that followed, he was abandoned by leaders of the Palestinian cause, state sponsors such as Libya who had protected and armed him, and his own friends. It was one of his own, a Swiss militant named Bruno Bréguet, who served as a CIA informant and provided details that helped lead to Carlos’s ultimate capture in Khartoum in 1994. By then, he was too hot, too disobedient, too undisciplined; the magazine profiles and careless lifestyle had caught up with him. The moment itself was anticlimactic: Instead of a dramatic shoot-out, he was detained while groggy from sedation after an operation to minimize pain in his groin. When Carlos was finally caught, it was as if one era was over and another, more horrific one began. It is fitting that his reign ended in Sudan. (“To describe the country’s political climate as permissive for terrorists would be to understate the case,” Warrick writes.) Sudan would also give bin Laden a safe haven until he was expelled in 1996 and forced to move al Qaeda’s operations to Afghanistan. Yet Carlos’s influence was never truly supplanted. Indeed, there is something disconcertingly familiar about the book, which makes it hard to shake a haunting feeling that we are playing the same record over and over. Carlos’s most lasting legacy was in treating violence as a performative act, a show with no plot. After all, by the time of his capture, he was nothing more than a paid mercenary. The Palestinian cause receded and was ultimately irrelevant to his actions. As Warrick recently wrote in the New York Times, Carlos’s “brand” of the terrorist-for-hire continues today with countries such as Russia and Iran paying criminal networks to do their global bidding by attacking political enemies in the West, getting what they want with plausible deniability. But Carlos’s love of the limelight also resonates today. In the age of social media, the filming and streaming of violence and death are ubiquitous. Lone wolves write manifestos as if they, too, are famous, worthy of attention, and motivated by a higher cause. When a healthcare executive is murdered, his killer becomes a kind of superstar. In the multiple assassination attempts on U.S. President Donald Trump, the alleged shooters didn’t even seem to have a clear political allegiance. Violence is performed for an audience, the spectacle, the symbolism. And while terror groups remain—including al Qaeda and groups with ties to it, such as Boko Haram—a lot of terrorist violence today is carried out by those who are just courting infamy. As Carlos realized his growing isolation after he was kicked out of the PFLP in 1975, he hoped to create a new terrorist group. His friend, upon hearing of Carlos’s plans, later remarked, “I knew it would never work. … [T]he man before me was no mastermind. He was an executioner.” Although Carlos failed at the one thing he wanted the most—for all of us to still care just how famous he was—the world that he unleashed continues to thrive in this era of branding, even if not under his banner. Bin Laden is dead, and the terror threat we face today is often more dispersed, random, and ideologically incoherent than in the al Qaeda founder’s time. There are plenty of executioners and no masterminds. A lot of people are watching, but for what purpose? Juliette Kayyem is a professor at Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government, where she is faculty chair of the homeland security project. An author and CNN senior national security analyst, she has previously served in senior counterterrorism and homeland security positions in state and federal government. She writes the Early Warning newsletter on Substack. X: @juliettekayyem Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: The Bab el-Mandeb Problem
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.46
The Bab el-Mandeb Problem Houthi control of a Red Sea port brings Tehran closer to claiming another critical waterway. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fight for control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, record-high global temperatures, and Ukraine’s request for more foreign aid. The Fall of Mokha Houthi rebels in Yemen seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday in their quest to eventually control the vital Bab el-Mandeb strait. The sweeping ground offensive—which pushed out forces allied with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government—raised concerns that the two sides’ fragile 2022 truce may officially be over and that Yemen has returned to all-out war. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fight for control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, record-high global temperatures, and Ukraine’s request for more foreign aid. The Fall of Mokha Houthi rebels in Yemen seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday in their quest to eventually control the vital Bab el-Mandeb strait. The sweeping ground offensive—which pushed out forces allied with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government—raised concerns that the two sides’ fragile 2022 truce may officially be over and that Yemen has returned to all-out war. Renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni forces erupted in July, after the Saudi-led military coalition tried to prevent a plane bringing Houthis back from Tehran from landing at Sanaa International Airport. Since then, the two sides have exchanged heavy fire, including a Saudi attack on a Houthi-run prison on Monday, which killed at least 23 people, and a Houthi operation across Saudi Arabia that same day, which injured more than 70 people. Fierce battles around Mokha in recent days have particularly drawn the international community’s attention, as many worry that Houthi control of the port brings Iran one step closer to claiming another critical waterway. For months, Iranian forces have effectively stopped most commercial traffic from transiting the Strait of Hormuz, through which around one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas previously passed. That has forced vessels to rely more heavily on Bab el-Mandeb, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. However, if the Houthis—an Iranian-backed proxy group—were to transform Bab el-Mandeb into a second choke point, then Tehran would likely turn the strait into another war front, further strangling the already volatile global energy market. Mokha is less than 50 miles from Bab el-Mandeb. Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate oil prices both exceeded $100 per barrel on Thursday in response to the Houthis’ assault. “This is a potentially major strategic shift,” Maged al-Madhaji, the co-founder of a Yemen-based think tank, the Sanaa Center, told FP’s Keith Johnson. “The fall of Mokha—and, increasingly, the prospect of Houthi control over Bab el-Mandeb—would allow them to turn intermittent pressure on shipping into a sustained threat at much lower operational cost.” What comes next remains unclear. Some experts suggest that the Houthis may try to seize Perim Island, a Yemeni territory that sits at the strait’s narrowest point, making it a crucial hub for controlling the flow of maritime traffic; already, the proxy group has reached the Red Sea islands of Hanish. Taking Perim, though, would grant the Houthis a similar position to Iran’s control of Larak Island, which Tehran uses to monitor global shipping and host military activity. On Wednesday, Pakistan warned Iran to rein in the Houthis’ actions or risk triggering a joint defense arrangement involving Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad. Today’s Most Read - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson What We’re Following Turn up the AC. August marked one of the world’s hottest months in recorded history, according to a new report by the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service on Thursday. With an average global surface air temperature of 1.65 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, August 2026 tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest period. Last month also saw the highest daily sea surface temperature over the extra-polar ocean (the band of ocean located between 60 degrees south and 60 degrees north latitude) ever recorded, and it wrapped up Europe’s warmest summer in recent history. Copernicus cited the burning of fossil fuels and a strong El Niño climate pattern for the rise in air and sea temperatures. Human-caused greenhouse gas emissions rose 0.7 percent globally last year to hit a record 54 billion tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, the European Commission said on Monday. The world’s top two emitters—China and the United States—each saw their climate pollution rates increase in 2025. These figures lend support to last week’s damning United Nations report, which warned that humanity has lost its chance to prevent some of the worst consequences of climate change, as the world has failed to achieve the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels. Zelensky seeks support. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on Thursday to discuss opportunities for greater foreign aid and collaboration. “The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter,” Zelensky wrote on X, referring to Russia’s repeated strategy of targeting civilian energy infrastructure during Ukraine’s coldest months. “We will discuss how to strengthen our resilience, support our people, and ensure that Ukraine has the capabilities it needs to defend itself.” Carney reaffirmed that sentiment on Thursday, adding that Canada “remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine’s defense, recovery, and reconstruction.” He vowed to deepen defense, economic, and energy cooperation, and he unveiled another critical air defense package that adds to the billions of dollars that Ottawa has already given Kyiv since the war began in February 2022. Zelensky’s trip to Canada concludes a week of foreign travel marred by difficulties. In a trip to Oslo on Tuesday for the funeral of Norwegian King Harald V, Zelensky’s connection at Moldova’s Chisinau International Airport was delayed due to a drone threat. It is unclear who launched the drone or how close it came to Zelensky’s plane, but Moldovan President Maia Sandu claimed on Wednesday that “a Russian drone forced us to close our airspace temporarily.” Economic woes. The European Central Bank raised its key interest rate by a quarter point on Thursday, bringing it to 2.5 percent—the highest level in more than a year. This was the bank’s second increase since the Iran war erupted in late February, and it signals growing concerns that the global energy crisis will keep inflation in Europe above its original 2 percent target through 2028. “The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period,” European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said, adding that the economic outlook going into next year remains “highly uncertain.” Still, Thursday’s increase was not a shock to economists, who expected a rate hike to coincide with recent skyrocketing global oil prices. Renewed fighting in the Middle East has put central banks under greater pressure, threatened critical global supply chains, and worsened bond market volatility. Next week, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan, and the U.S. Federal Reserve will separately meet to determine their own interest rates. Traders are predicting that all three banks will increase their rates. Odds and Ends Two men, two shovels, and one pit of dirt. Nineteen teams of two gathered in the northern Hungarian town of Nyergesujfalu on Saturday for a grave-digging competition. Organized by the Hungarian Association of Cemetery Maintainers and Operators, the contest for the quickest-dug and most stylish grave aimed to show off this vital trade skill and counter taboos surrounding death. Diggers Robert Nagy and Laszlo Kiss took first place with a winning time of 1 hour and 21 minutes, receiving a cash prize of roughly $640. item.title: Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.17
Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire Failed wars are predictable, if you know what to look for. In a world where great-power competition is intensifying, a revealing test of foreign-policy acumen is a country’s ability to avoid costly conflicts or other endeavors that waste resources, divert attention, and ultimately leave them weaker rather than stronger. In other words: staying out of quagmires. Great powers are often happy to see their rivals stumble into strategic quicksand and may even try to encourage such developments, but wise leaders try to stay out of this kind of trouble. In recent decades, China has done a far better job of avoiding quagmires than either the United States or Russia. Post-Cold War hubris led U.S. leaders to take on a vast array of global responsibilities, some that made sense but many that did not. The “forever wars” in Iraq and Afghanistan are the most obvious examples of the latter, of course, but the United States also gotten itself mired in lesser conflicts in Libya, Yemen, Syria, and various parts of Africa, largely as part of the “global war on terror.” In a world where great-power competition is intensifying, a revealing test of foreign-policy acumen is a country’s ability to avoid costly conflicts or other endeavors that waste resources, divert attention, and ultimately leave them weaker rather than stronger. In other words: staying out of quagmires. Great powers are often happy to see their rivals stumble into strategic quicksand and may even try to encourage such developments, but wise leaders try to stay out of this kind of trouble. In recent decades, China has done a far better job of avoiding quagmires than either the United States or Russia. Post-Cold War hubris led U.S. leaders to take on a vast array of global responsibilities, some that made sense but many that did not. The “forever wars” in Iraq and Afghanistan are the most obvious examples of the latter, of course, but the United States also gotten itself mired in lesser conflicts in Libya, Yemen, Syria, and various parts of Africa, largely as part of the “global war on terror.” One might add the long, inept, and fruitless effort to broker an Israeli-Palestinian peace, which consumed vast amounts of presidential time and attention and ultimately failed, in good part because Washington acted not as a fair-minded mediator but as “Israel’s lawyer.” And now U.S. President Donald Trump has walked open-eyed into a quagmire of his own making with Iran, one with few if any benefits, increasingly obvious costs, and no obvious exit save a humiliating retreat. Similarly, since 2000, Russia has engaged in a series of frozen conflicts with various neighbors, failed to prop up clients such as former Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych or former Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad, and is now mired the running sore of war in Ukraine. Not only have these actions cost the Russian economy and the Russian people a great deal, but they have also poisoned relations with most of Europe and made Russia increasingly dependent on China. Both Washington and Moscow had reasons for acting as they did, but it is hard to argue that these various adventures left either country in a stronger global position. By contrast, China has stayed out of costly quagmires and focused on building power at home, constructing islands in the South China Sea, expanding its diplomatic presence and influence abroad, insulating itself from foreign pressure by building up stockpiles and reserves, and gaining leverage through its control of raw earths and other parts of global supply chains. To be sure, its growing military power and increasingly assertive foreign policy have alarmed its neighbors and encouraged them to balance against Beijing, but its overall position vis-à-vis both Russia and the United States has improved considerably. China’s approach suggests that staying out of trouble abroad is a pretty smart strategy. So why do states blunder into quagmires, and how might they avoid them in the future? Here are some of the warning signs. Ignorance. Nobody starts a war that they think will be long, costly, and maybe end with being defeated. It follows that if they had known in advance what they were getting into, most leaders would have tried something else. And that suggests that quagmires usually arise from ignorance about the country you’re taking on, the difficulties you will encounter against them, or the ways that other actors will respond. The lesson: If you’re about to intervene in a country that you know very little about, look out. Bad advice. Decisions to intervene don’t arise from thin air; somebody has to come up with the idea and then convince the people in charge to embrace it. If you want to avoid a quagmire, therefore, you should be deeply skeptical of the advice you’ll get from self-interested parties who have their own reasons for wanting you to intervene. It was a mistake for the Bush administration to listen to pro-war Iraqi exiles such as Ahmed Chalabi, who wanted to ride to power on the back of the U.S. military. It was equally foolish for Trump to believe Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s sales pitch for a war with Iran, or to have paid attention to similar blandishments from pro-war voices in the United States. This problem is nothing new. In his Discourses on Livy, Niccolò Machiavelli specifically warns leaders against taking the testimony of self-interested parties (in his case, exiles) too seriously: “How vain the faith and promises of men are who are exiles from their own country. … Such is their extreme desire to return to their homes that they naturally believe many things that are not true, and add many others on purpose; so that, with what they really believe and what they say they believe, they will fill you with hopes to that degree that if you attempt to act upon them, you will incur a fruitless expense, or engage in an undertaking that will involve you in ruin.” Notice that the first two problems reinforce each other. The more ignorant one is, the greater the tendency to accept the advice of those who claim to know what is going on. Groupthink. States are also more likely to stumble into quagmires when options aren’t debated in a clear and fair-minded way. Overconfident autocrats surrounded by sycophants and loyalists (think Russian President Vladimir Putin or Trump) are prone to making mistakes of this kind, but so are leaders who refuse to listen to dissenting views and are prone to ignoring information that doesn’t fit their preconceived notions. We all have a tendency to overvalue evidence that supports what we want to do and to discount evidence that we’re wrong, which is why leaders seeking to avoid a quagmire should work overtime to hear alternative views and encourage advisors to stress-test the assumptions underlying the case for war. When leaders don’t do this, the combination of ignorance, bad advice, and a biased decision-making process can lead directly to… Overconfidence. Ignorance and bad advice typically combine to persuade decision-makers that success will be easy to achieve, either because the opponent is militarily inferior, its government is fragile and will quickly collapse, the local population is restive and will welcome the invader, or some combination of the above. Sometimes these things are true, but not often, and managing the aftermath of victory can be even more challenging than the purely military task of defeating an inferior foe. If you want to avoid a quagmire, therefore, make sure you have carefully considered what you are going to do if you win. Even more important, make sure you have a Plan B if your best-case theory of victory turns out to be wrong and you find yourself facing a protracted fight. Unreliable local partners. The U.S. experience in Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq, and now Iran teach a similar lesson: Quagmires are hard to avoid when you don’t have competent and reliable local partners. Washington devoted vast sums trying to nation-build in the first three cases, but its local clients were divided, corrupt, and had their own agendas. Trump seems to have believed that unhappy Iranians (of which there are many) would rise up if the regime’s top leaders were gone, a fantasy that entirely ignored the regime’s well-organized security forces and the lack of a well-organized opposition. Putin made a similar miscalculation in thinking that the Ukrainian government would dissolve as soon as his forces crossed the border (or be easily replaced by pro-Russian quislings once the invading force reached Kyiv), a vain hope that revealed his failure to appreciate the intensity of Ukrainian national feeling. Once it is clear that the optimistic prewar expectations were false and that the war will be long and difficult, a new set of problems comes into play. Even if the smart thing to do is to cut one’s losses and disengage, there are at least two obvious reasons why leaders often find it difficult to extricate themselves from a costly quagmire. Credibility concerns. Governments often believe that they must “stay the course” to preserve a reputation for steadfastness and reliability. Former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger knew the United States couldn’t win in Vietnam, for example, and even conceded that it might have been better if the United States had never entered the war. But he insisted that the commitment of 500,000 U.S. troops had “settled the issue of the importance of” Vietnam because he believed—incorrectly—that withdrawing would undermine U.S. credibility and cause other allies to abandon Washington. He knew the war was lost and that Vietnam was of marginal strategic importance, but his obsession with credibility helped prolong the war for six more years. And as Daniel Ellsberg argued in a famous essay, there is a domestic political analogue here. Leaders are often reluctant to extricate themselves from quagmires because they fear the domestic political consequences of an obvious failure. Even when they know that victory is unlikely, they prefer to kick the can down the road and hand the problem off to their successor. U.S. President Lyndon Johnson passed Vietnam on to Richard Nixon, and Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Trump each bequeathed Afghanistan to the person who replaced them. President Joe Biden had the courage to end a war that he understood the United States was unlikely to win but was widely criticized for the (inevitably) chaotic outcome that accompanied the U.S. withdrawal. This may also be why Trump won’t simply cut his losses and end the war with Iran: He’s still hoping that he can achieve something he might be able to package as a “victory.” Good luck with that. Ironically, this fear of domestic political consequences may be misplaced. Saddam Hussein ended the foolish war that he had started with Iran after eight years of fighting and didn’t fall from power, and he remained in charge in Iraq even after his humiliating defeat in the first Gulf War. President Ronald Reagan withdrew from Lebanon after more than 240 U.S. service members were killed in a terrorist bombing, but he was still widely regarded as a tough-minded, hawkish president. Even Biden suffered little long-term damage from disengaging from Afghanistan in his first year in office—that early decision played hardly any role in the 2024 campaign or in Kamala Harris’s subsequent loss. “Victory is just around the corner.” Powerful states also remain stuck in quagmires because they can afford to keep fighting, and because they have the wherewithal to keep trying new approaches. “There’s a lot of ruin in a nation,” wrote Adam Smith, and that’s especially true for countries with large populations and large economies. Even when the stakes are not that great and victory seems unlikely, a great power can keep a dumb war going for a long time, especially if it can rely on an all-volunteer force, run deficits instead of raising taxes, and keep trying new strategies or new weapons in the hope that one of them will provide the key to victory. Look at all the different things that Russia (and Ukraine) have tried over the past four years, or the various options and strategic innovations that the United States attempted during the various quagmires that it has stumbled into. Thus, Americans were repeatedly told that they had “turned the corner” in Vietnam, a mantra that was resurrected and repeated in Iraq and Afghanistan. In the former, Washington tried coercive bombing, an invasion of Cambodia, mining North Vietnamese harbors, widespread use of defoliants such as Agent Orange, the construction of “strategic hamlets” to protect the local population, “Vietnamization,” etc., all to no avail. The 2007 “surge” in Iraq brought some short-term military benefits but failed to resolve the country’s broader political problems, and the analogous Afghanistan “surge” that the Pentagon foisted on Obama in 2009 was equally unsuccessful. Wealthy states can keep trying different options for a long time, and it is always at least remotely possible that a bit more effort will yield success. Upon such hopes are quagmires prolonged. The bottom line is that quagmires occur because getting out of a war is harder than getting into one. If one wants to avoid quagmires, therefore, a deep-seated reluctance to get involved in foreign wars is one’s best protection. States still need capable military forces and a population that is willing to fight to defend truly vital interests, but pursuing wars of choice fought for flimsy or marginal reasons, on the assumption that they will be easy, is a good way to find yourself in conflicts that you can neither win nor easily end. Thus far, Chinese President Xi Jinping and his associates seem to understand this principle better than Trump and many of his predecessors. As long as that remains the case, advantage Beijing. Stephen M. Walt is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Robert and Renée Belfer professor of international relations at Harvard University. Walt is the author of The New Geopolitics, a five-part newsletter masterclass breaking down the biggest concepts you should use to navigate today’s world.
