When she was in residency training, she said, she experienced what felt like a “stampede of wild horses” across her chest and was convinced that she had a heart problem—until her doctors, having conducted a battery of tests, recommended that she seriously consider chilling out. And many components of somatic practice have evidence to back them up. Interoception, or awareness of one’s own physical signals, really can be important for well-being—perhaps because it increases people’s sense of attunement with their body, connection with the present moment, or agency over otherwise vague and inscrutable sensations. Mindfulness meditation, which involves interoception, has been shown to decrease stress and anxiety and even reduce physical pain. Yoga and breathing exercises can decrease amygdala activation and lead to better concentration, memory, and executive function. But the somatics packaging of these techniques is alluring partly because of the emotional liberation it promises. Somaticists tend to describe a clear path: identify a physical signal, connect it to its psychic cause, then let it go. If the nervous system overactivates, surely you can just reset it. If the body holds trauma, surely the body can relinquish it. These were always just metaphors, though, and imperfect ones. The amygdala doesn’t have a reboot button. There is no viscous gunk of emotional pain to flush out. The Body Keeps the Score has been somewhat debunked; critics have argued that van der Kolk incorrectly described certain studies, and that he seems to have made up others entirely. (Responding to the writer Emi Nietfeld’s critique in Mother Jones, van der Kolk said that at times he drew on unpublished data.) Trauma experts have pushed back on his wholesale condemnation of talk therapy, which can be, according to a mountain of evidence, very helpful for treating PTSD. There’s also something ironic in how certain somaticists—ostensibly advocates for the mind-body connection—talk as if the two are separated by a nearly unbridgeable gap: the physical burden of trauma unreachable through thinking or conversation, and perhaps not even accessible to conscious awareness. So somatics isn’t a miracle cure. And it’s probably right to be skeptical of influencers who seek to collect on people’s need to feel at home in their body. But that doesn’t mean somatics can’t be helpful. Much of it, after all, turns out to be pretty straightforward. Movement is good, generally. Breathing is good. Stepping away from your screen—stretching your limbs, remembering you are real and tangible and mortal—is good. When I signed up for that somatic-exercise class, I expected that I might leave rolling my eyes, but I secretly hoped I’d walk out lighter, more alive and connected to myself and the world. What I found was something in between. The actual workout couldn’t have been more basic: It consisted largely of squats, jumping jacks, crunches, some yoga—downward dog, child’s pose. Occasionally the instructor would remind us to check in with our bodies: “What are you being invited into? And I don’t mean the burpee.” Or: “Let the chin enter the conversation.” Otherwise it hardly seemed uniquely somatic, or uniquely anything. Then again, I had the post-workout endorphin glow. I’d left my apartment and shut my phone in a locker. An hour later, I exited the studio somewhat baffled. But walking out onto a busy Manhattan street, I felt a little more conscious of the sun on my cheek, the solidness of the ground pushing against my feet. This was silly, I thought. And also: Maybe I’ll come back. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic

item.title: Japan’s Strategic Turn
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Score: 4.18
When I first visited Japan more than 30 years ago, the Cold War had ended, China had not yet risen, and the country—although it was no longer the Japan as Number One of Ezra Vogel’s best-selling 1979 book—was formidable. Japan’s GDP was not very far behind that of the United States, was larger than that of most of the rest of Asia combined, and was seven times that of China. On a recent visit, I found a very different country. Even in 1995, there were ominous signs: the collapse of property prices and several years—which would stretch into decades—of economic stagnation. Birth rates were below replacement, at roughly 1.4 per woman, although they have since fallen further, to a bit more than 1.1. But some of the biggest changes lie in Japan’s geopolitical environment. Today, Japan’s GDP is roughly a fifth of China’s, and although the size of its armed forces remains roughly the same as in the past, it is now far outstripped by that of its continental neighbor. Back in 1995, North Korea was still a decade away from testing a nuclear weapon; today, it has dozens or even scores of weapons that it can deliver. And back then, Russia was still recovering from its rocky transition out of Communist rule; today, it is aligned with China and routinely provides military technology to China and North Korea. Small wonder that the Japanese political, military, and intelligence leaders as well as academic experts I recently spoke with were grim. They cling to their security treaty with the United States, but their government is also doing once-unthinkable things to ensure their own defense. For most of the postwar period, Japan relied on its defense treaty with the Americans and on robust economic growth. Defense spending was held at 1 percent of GDP, but its economy was so much larger than those of its neighbors that this meant a relatively substantial investment in the Japan Self-Defense Forces. Despite its love of samurai movies and martial arts, Japan remained a pacifist country that did not export weapons, focused on defensive missions, and pledged not to produce, possess, or host nuclear weapons. All of that has changed. Under plans adopted in 2022, Japan has increased its defense spending to something like 1.4 percent of GDP, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has indicated that it will rise to 2 percent. It is likely to go beyond that, possibly even as far as the 3.5 percent target now generally accepted in Europe. The result is not just an improvement of Japanese weapons systems across the board (numbers of service personnel remaining stable), but the acquisition of new capabilities. Japan is now openly acquiring what it calls “counterstrike” weapons—that is, missiles of various kinds that can hit targets on the Chinese mainland. It is investing in cyber and space operations, as well as in much greater air and missile defenses. It is building concrete shelters and digging tunnels for passive defense against Chinese attacks on its bases, something that the United States has inexplicably failed to do in either Asia or the Middle East. Japan is newly willing to sustain its defense industries by exporting weapons. This year it created its first centralized intelligence agency—the National Intelligence Bureau—since World War II. Most interesting of all is the shift in Japanese attitudes to nuclear weapons. The Japanese policy toward those weapons after World War II was grounded in the trauma of being the only country to have suffered a nuclear attack. On this trip, I heard nary a word about Hiroshima or Nagasaki but a great deal about deterrence. More to the point, Japanese officials and experts were virtually unanimous on the need to drop at least one of the three legs of its nuclear policy: the prohibition of introducing nuclear weapons on Japanese soil. They were eager to explore the possibility of arrangements with the United States comparable to those with Germany or other European countries, under which both countries have their finger on the nuclear button, a so-called dual key. A submarine-launched cruise missile with a nuclear warhead, now under development in the U.S., seems to be the preferred system. Japan could easily develop nuclear weapons. It has ample supplies of plutonium and outstanding engineers. It would much prefer not to, for a host of reasons, including lingering domestic opposition and fear of preemptive attack. But the arguments I heard against a purely Japanese nuclear deterrent are now cast in prudential terms, not emotional or historical ones. These changes emerge from a heightened Japanese sense of threat. Almost every day, Chinese coast-guard vessels enter the contiguous zone (12 to 24 miles out) around the Senkaku Islands, which stretch almost to Taiwan, and they commonly intrude into Japanese territorial waters there. The Chinese coast guard, it should be noted, has vessels the size of frigates or destroyers in other navies, and that have mounted automatic cannons of the type used for combat rather than law enforcement. Their belligerent rhetoric upon encountering their Japanese counterparts matches that of their government. Joint Chinese and Russian air patrols unnerve Japan’s air defenders, as do increasing flights of Chinese drones near Japanese islands. China’s insistence that the Senkaku Islands are Chinese is of long standing but has become more strident in recent years. Meanwhile, Japan looks with dismay at a China whose nuclear arsenal is growing quickly, as is that of North Korea. And both are aligned with a Russia whose navy and air force remain active in the Pacific despite the demands of the fighting in Ukraine. Japan is in a tough spot, and for that and other reasons, its attitude to the United States is different from that of many European countries. In Japan, one seldom hears complaints about democratic backsliding or accusations of betrayal. Rather, the Japanese are desperate to put their faith in the U.S. at a time when alternatives are few. There is no Pacific NATO, and even the combined command of U.S. and Japanese forces is not nearly as organizationally robust as that of the United States and South Korea. There is only the presence of American forces (oriented for the most part toward Korea and Taiwan) and America’s good word, as well as Japan’s determination to resist encroachment—or, as its defense documents call it, “invasion”—by a hostile China. Japan’s anxieties around Taiwan are high. Even a peaceful takeover of the island by China would represent a major setback. It would unhinge Japan’s and the United States’ strategic posture in East Asia, and encourage (in Japan’s view) accommodation or worse from some of China’s neighbors. In a seemingly spontaneous remark in late 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi indicated that a Chinese naval blockade of Taiwan would count as a “survival-threatening situation” that would, by implication, permit Japan’s use of force for collective self-defense. Despite the furor that erupted, she has not withdrawn those remarks. The next few years may be perilous in East Asia if China sees an opportunity created by a distracted and underequipped America to accomplish its goal of unifying an unwilling Taiwan with the mainland. Thankfully, the U.S.-Japan relationship is an alliance that the Trump administration has not yet heedlessly and willfully damaged. For the sake not only of Tokyo but of peace in the region, one hopes that will remain the case.

item.title: The Netherlands Will Never Be Rid of Louisiana Crawfish
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Science Score: 4.65
Confronted with a seasoned, boiled, arguably delicious crayfish, some of the people of the Netherlands are not sure exactly what to do. “Do you suck the head out?” I heard from the table next to me earlier this summer, at Two Chefs, a restaurant in Amsterdam that hosts a monthly crayfish boil.
Yes is the answer: The best way to eat a crayfish is to shell the tail, then slurp the flavored juices out of the head, and pick out the remaining meat with your hands. This strategy might not be an immediate transatlantic hit. At the boil, one 29-year-old from Maastricht likened the meal to shrimp but with more work. Two twins told me that the crayfish would need to look a little more chic on the plate to appeal to the Dutch public. But, given the ever-growing population of crayfish in the Netherlands, coming around to eating more of them could benefit the country. Because if Dutch consumers aren’t sure how they feel about crayfish, crayfish inarguably love the Netherlands. They have invaded the country’s waterways so thoroughly that they have become a real problem, and dealing with them will mean persuading more creatures—including Dutch people—to eat more crayfish. The crayfish invasion started decades ago, but in recent years, the red swamp crayfish (also known as the Louisiana crawfish) has become a particular pest, Pim Lemmers, an ecologist at Radboud University who has dedicated his career to researching crayfish, told me. In the 1980s, it was brought to the Netherlands as food, and people naively released the animals into the environment. The waterways in the Netherlands are very interconnected and became a “crayfish highway” of sorts, Ivo Roessink, an aquatic ecotoxicologist at Wageningen University & Research, told me. But crayfish can walk and breathe on land, too, and have been spotted in parks, along bike lanes, and at Schiphol airport, where the birds use the runway to crush them. And they can dig—burrows up to three feet long that can collapse the edges of fields into the water and that some people fear could damage the country’s extensive system of dams, dikes, and canals. Scientists emphasize that the risk to dams and dikes is low; from their point of view, the bigger risk is to other creatures that live in the water. Crayfish are omnivorous: “They totally destroy underwater vegetation,” Roessink said. They also eat detritus, amphibian and insect larvae, snails and other invertebrates, small fish, and one another—a sight I witnessed for myself. But crayfish cannibalism will not end the invasion; in fact, although the Netherlands’ central government is working on a program for crayfish management, getting rid of the species will likely be impossible. “I know of one example where they effectively eradicated crayfish, and that was in the U.S.,” Roessink said. “There was an infected pond, and they turned it into a parking lot.” (Resorting to this solution in the Netherlands would require paving over the entire country.) Research in the Netherlands and elsewhere has shown that even extensive trapping won’t necessarily eliminate crayfish. The most anyone can hope for is fewer of them. Some water boards of the Netherlands are trying to persuade all sorts of creatures to eat more crayfish, including herons, eels, and European catfish, which are themselves something of an invasive threat. And, in theory, one of the crayfish’s most effective predators could be Dutch people. Stefan van Ekris and Maarten van der Sanden, who are both managing directors at CrawFish Farm Holland, are trying their best to make it happen. This July, I joined them as they put on waders and immersed themselves in irrigation ditches to set and check their crayfish nets in the Groene Hart, or “Green Heart,” of the Netherlands, the thinly populated pastures and peatlands among some of the country’s largest cities. They get paid per kilogram caught—the expedition I joined yielded about 150 kilograms, or 330 pounds, of live crayfish—but this is really a passion project for them. CrawFish Farm Holland is approved to sell live and prepared catch directly to restaurants and other wholesalers, and hopes to sell its crayfish in supermarkets in the next two years. “We’re not cultivating them,” Van der Sanden told me. “We’re fighting them and eating them.” In America, Van der Sanden pointed out, Louisiana was able to quickly ramp up crayfish production and demand in the 1980s. But the scientists I spoke with were skeptical of this strategy. “You will never eat yourself out of this crisis,” Roessink said. And if people like crayfish too much, Lemmers said, they might start cultivating crayfish in their backyard or trapping them without oversight, which could promote further spread. Even if more Dutch people come around to the pleasures of a messy boil, the crayfish still could come out ahead. The image originally accompanying this article did not show a red swamp crayfish. That image has been replaced.

item.title: How — and why — to tell your doctor you’re feeling depressed
item.description:
Source: Vox Score: 2.46
We’re making this story accessible to all readers as a public service. Support our journalism by becoming a member today. I don’t know about you, but whenever I go to see my primary care doctor, my mental health isn’t usually at the top of my list of things to talk about. But it should be. In fact, experts say that all of us could benefit from more candid conversations with our doctors about our mental health. (This story discusses mental health issues and suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You are not alone. You can call the national 988 hotline for support.) For years, the United States has been trying to figure out “parity” for mental health care — to have it treated and paid for like any other medical need, not something that is carved out and separate. A big part of that has been pushing primary care doctors and OB/GYNs to do more screenings, to make your mental state a part of your well-being that you discuss with your doctor the same as your blood pressure or any physical ailment. But that is easier said than done. A lot of people may not even realize that their depression or anxiety or stress is something they should talk about with their primary care doctor. Others might fear being judged, and for good reason — national policymakers warn there continues to be a stigma toward mental health conditions among doctors. About one in three Americans say they have never been asked about their mental health by a doctor, which is unsettling considering that the nation has been going through a collective mental health crisis for several years. Men are significantly less likely to be asked about their mental health than women — perhaps a reflection of a culture that expects men to “tough it out” when it comes to their feelings. But those attitudes come with a price: Men are diagnosed with depression at half the rate as women, but die by suicide much more frequently. Much of the burden for starting these conversations should fall on your doctor to be more curious and accommodating during annual exams. But you don’t have to wait to be asked to bring it up. Regularly talking to your provider about your mental health is the best way to get ahead of any problems and get treated if you need to be. In honor of Suicide Prevention Month, I reached out to a handful of doctors who have studied why it’s sometimes so hard for patients and doctors to talk about depression, anxiety, and stress — and learned some novel strategies for how you can take charge, push through any stigma, and start having more honest talks with your doctor about your state of mind. Here’s what you should know. Know the relevant symptoms before you talk to your doctor One of the tricky things about depression or any serious mental health problem is that it isn’t always easy to identify when you’re the one experiencing it. “Patients need to recognize their distress…as potentially emanating from depression,” Dr. Richard Kravitz, a general medicine professor at UC Davis who has studied depression screening in primary care, told me. There is a checklist of sorts that you can go through on your own to understand whether you’re just having a tough couple of days or there’s something more serious at work, said Dr. Maria Garcia, an internal medicine physician at UC San Francisco. You might be feeling down or unmotivated or have a lack of energy, or be more agitated, angry, or irritable than usual. Sometimes there are less obvious signs, like trouble with money or problems at work. Symptoms of depression Here are some of the possible signs of depression, according to the Mayo Clinic. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You can call the national 988 hotline for support. - Feeling sad or hopeless or like you are a burden to others - Feeling more irritable and angry than usual, losing your temper more easily - Losing interest in most or all normal day-to-day activities and hobbies - Sleep problems, whether you are sleeping too little or too much - Feeling less energetic than usual - Changes in appetite — whether you are eating less and losing weight or eating more and gaining weight - Concentration and memory problems - Unexplained physical symptoms “If you’re not getting enjoyment from your normal hobbies or talking to the people that you would normally really enjoy talking to, if you find yourself isolating from people that you normally really enjoy spending time with, I think those are certainly triggers,” she said. Consider the duration of your symptoms, too: “If it’s every day for a couple of weeks, that definitely isn’t normal.” And oftentimes, depression symptoms can mirror symptoms of other ailments or problems, like a lack of sleep, low appetite, or physical aches and pains. This is one reason why it is so important to talk with your doctor about it, Garcia said. Is that fatigue a result of depression — or is it a problem with your thyroid? Your primary care physician is best positioned to help you figure that out. One of the benefits of a long-term relationship with a physician is that they may be able to help you recognize symptoms of depression even if they aren’t obvious to you. It’s hard to be that self-aware; I’m certainly not all the time. But the more you pay attention to your mood and how it’s affecting your life, the more you can tell your doctor about what’s really going on. You don’t have to know all the fancy clinical terms, said Paul Duberstein, a clinical psychologist and professor of health behavior, society, and policy at the Rutgers School of Public Health. “The language that people are most comfortable using are words like stress or frustrated or impatient or something like that,” Duberstein told me. “Those are the kinds of things we really do want to incentivize and encourage people to talk to their doctors about.” How to bring up your mental health with your doctor Okay, you feel like something might be off and you have a doctor’s appointment coming up. What do you do? You might not have to do anything. These days, you are likely to be given a depression screening by your physician’s office before you ever arrive (usually as part of your pre-visit paperwork). Garcia said it’s important to be honest and to be thorough when answering those questions, as that will tell your doctor that your mental health should be a focus for your upcoming visit. Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American healthcare policy. Sign up here. But if you aren’t proactively screened for depression and you have some of the symptoms described above or you just have a hunch that something might be wrong, try to alert your doctor in advance that your mental health is something you want to talk about. If that’s not possible, tell your doctor early on in the appointment that your mental state is something you want to discuss. Garcia said that, rightly or wrongly, doctors can sometimes be reluctant to dive deep into a discussion about mental health late into a visit; they only have so much time with individual patients, and they might balk at trying to squeeze in a mental health discussion at the end. The conversation is more likely to be productive if you proactively start it before your physician is sidetracked with your blood sugar. During this conversation, you can ask for a depression screening outright. Doctors have become adept at recognizing code words; if you say your mood has been off, they may pick up the signal that you may be experiencing mental health struggles. But there is a good argument for being very direct about how you’re feeling, Kravitz said. “My advice…is just simply to say to the doctor, ‘I’ve been feeling down’ or ‘I’ve been feeling irritable’ or ‘I’ve been losing sleep’ or ‘Something’s wrong and I don’t know what it is. Do you think it might be depression?’ Just ask,” Kravitz said. If you aren’t sure if it’s a mental or physical issue, tell them that. Activate your doctor’s curiosity, Kravitz told me. Get them invested in figuring out what’s going on with you. Once the conversation starts, your doctor is likely to ask how long you have been experiencing symptoms and how they are affecting your day-to-day function. When that happens, you should be as thorough and truthful as possible. “Is it affecting your ability to take care of your family? Is it affecting your ability to go to work, get up in the morning, cook dinner, get out of the house, go grocery shopping?” Garcia said. “Those things are really helpful because then we can tailor the treatments for the amount of functional impairment.” Talk to your doctor about your sleep, too, Duberstein said. Not only is it an important indicator of your physical health, but it will also tell your doctor something about your mental well-being. And it doesn’t require any special emotional vocabulary: You probably know if you’re sleeping well or not. “If you think about major depression as a collection of, say, nine symptoms and you ask, ‘Well, what symptoms appear first? Is it the depressed mood? Or the difficulty concentrating?’ The first thing that appears typically is sleep,” Duberstein told me. “Disrupted sleep is something that I think people do feel comfortable talking with their doctor about.” How to talk to your doctor about a treatment plan If you have a productive conversation with your doctor and they recognize symptoms of depression, they’ll want to establish a treatment plan. This has historically been another barrier to honest conversations between doctors and patients about mental health: Patients don’t want to be prescribed antidepressants or referred to therapy, so they don’t bring it up. But ignoring your symptoms is, of course, not the solution. Instead, use your appointment as an opportunity to ask all of your questions to make sure that you are fully comfortable with the doctor’s proposed treatment plan and can get on the road to better mental health. Many Americans have doubts about antidepressants, which have been egged on by high-profile figures like US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. If you’re hesitant to take meds, you should tell your provider about the things that you’ve heard that give you pause, the negative experiences people have shared, or whatever major questions or concerns you have. They can help you understand the very real trade-offs that come with taking an antidepressant, Kravitz said. Your doctor can also debunk some of the misconceptions that make people hesitant to take these drugs even when they are struggling. “The duration of therapy sometimes surprises people. But no, it doesn’t mean that you’ll have to be on it forever. No, most people don’t have serious withdrawal symptoms. Those can usually be managed by careful tapering if necessary and so on,” Kravitz said. He said you can ask your doctor outright: “What can I expect to happen over time? How long will I need to be on this?” If you’d rather not go on medication immediately, that’s totally valid. Your doctor may instead be able to help you find a therapist with a referral, Duberstein said. Therapists have historically been hard to find in the US — but one positive outcome of the pandemic was the proliferation of online mental health services. “I think it’s important for the public to know that one of the major barriers to getting into psychotherapy or even seeing a therapist — like getting into your car, driving, finding a bus, finding a subway, whatever — that those barriers are gone,” he told me. “Because you could see a therapist online now in all 50 states.” The goal is that you leave your doctor’s office feeling heard and feeling on-board with the approach, even if you still have some trepidation (which is very common). And if you don’t feel comfortable talking to your doctor about these issues, that may be a sign you need to find a new provider whom you feel you can trust with those sensitive discussions, Duberstein said. The point is, your doctor should be your ally in pursuing whatever treatment you need for whatever ails for your mental health. Nobody has to go through it alone.

item.title: How to find a date in real life
item.description:
Source: Vox Score: 2.03
If you want to hear someone complain, one of your best bets is to ask one of your single friends what the dating landscape is like right now. You’ll hear tales of first dates that lead nowhere, conversations that feel like they were ripped from a social media feed, and more and more people resigning themselves to partnerless existence. Even what once seemed like an ever-flowing fount of new romantic possibilities has now dried up: It feels like the days of meeting The One via a dating app are behind us. We are officially in a romantic slump. As dating coach Lily Womble explains: “Dating can be so exhausting, depleting, demoralizing, and I only think dating apps have increased that experience for single folks.” Despite how discouraging it can be, though, a lot of people still desire partnership. Womble is the author of Thank You, More Please: A Feminist Guide to Breaking Dumb Dating Rules and Finding Love, and she spoke with Vox about how to overcome dating fatigue. “If you do want to find love in a romantic partnership, there is a more healthful and empowering way to go about it that centers you as the main character,” she explains. So how do you center yourself? How do you take your dating life off of your phone and into the real world? We answer those questions and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Womble, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545. If you’re used to dating apps and you want to meet someone in person, how do you make that happen? Dating in person is a lost art of social connection. I think that our reliance on dating apps has made us all sicker in some ways. These apps are built like slot machines. They’re designed to keep you sitting there with a gallon bag full of quarters and a Big Gulp, hoping to pull the triple cherry and get lucky. It’s really important to reset your brain [from] dating apps, to get in-person to build new connections. It is as simple and as complicated as three steps. What are the steps? Number one: joy-building. Joy is connective. You need to exit your house, get off your couch, and go do something in your town or city that brings you some amount of joy with other people. It could be something free or something paid. The point is not to be in proximity to hotties at this event. The point is to make a new friendship, to make a new connection, to say, “Hey, how’s it going?” From there, you’re expanding your social circle. The function of a dating app is purely to expand your social circle and expand your opportunity window to meet somebody. Same with expanding your social circle with joy-building. You never know which 70-year-old you meet at your quilting night in your small town, whose son’s boyfriend’s cousin comes to a party and suddenly you’ve met the love of your life. I met my husband through joy-building. I went to an improv class, I made a friend that introduced me to her social circle, then I met Chris, my husband. Joy-building helps you meet the right people. Second, you’ve got co-conspiratorship: helping your friends help you better. Now, your friend might say, “I don’t know any single people.” To that, you say, “I don’t either. So let’s co-create creative solutions. We’re both smart. You have a workplace, you have a work conference. Are you looking out for me there? Here’s the kind of person that I’m looking for. Here’s the questions I want you to ask somebody.” Two of my clients were each other’s co-conspirators. They lived in different states. That didn’t matter because one of them visited the other, and in the airport met an eligible man, asked the qualifying and disqualifying questions, found out he was single, that he was eligible, that he was a good fit, and set them up. They literally started dating. So you need to have co-conspirators, you need to have friends looking out for you. Just like your friend asked you to be in their wedding, you need to ask them to support you in this way too. Finally, we’ve got flirting, which is the most vomitous, nerve-wracking part of this plan. The good news is that it’s a buildable skill set. It’s not just something that your favorite friend who is so naturally flirty has and you don’t. I think that flirting is essentially a joyful, courageous connection. People overcomplicate flirting to be this game. But I really believe, and have seen in my own experience, that flirting is just simply approaching somebody, asking a genuine question, and seeing if that person wants to co-create a conversation with you. To see if it’s romantic, you just ask, “Hey, random question. So are you single?” All of this requires 10 seconds of courage to go up to somebody and say, “Hey, you’re cute. I just wanted to come tell you that.” One of my clients did that on a crosswalk with a man that she found cute and they ended up dating. You make it sound so easy, but that joy-building, that getting out and talking to people, that can be really hard. One, it’s hard to be joyful when it feels like the world is falling apart around us. Also, some of us are more shy than others. And there are people who lost a lot of valuable flirt skill-building time during the pandemic. I hear you, but how do you do it? We have lost a lot of social skills. Those years that we were in lockdown were reps missed, especially for Gen Z, who literally were in school during that time. I’m a millennial, so I had already cut my teeth in New York circa 2015 with IRL flirting. It does require a rejection resilience plan. I recommend that people have in the notes app on their phone a plan to be courageous and to know how they’re going to react and care for themselves after a hard moment. There are people, when you flirt or joy-build, who don’t want to be your friend, who don’t want to talk to you, who are uncomfortable themselves. That rejection resilience plan can really prepare you to be courageous and to know that no matter what, you’re going to be okay. It’s as simple as understanding that your brain’s going to think it’s dying after an experience of rejection. Just say, “I think I’m going to die after rejection. It’s a thought, not a fact.” Then have a plan to be compassionate towards yourself. Self-compassion isn’t just a fluffy phrase. It is a science-backed tool that decreases cortisol, and increases resilience. I also recommend a flirting ladder to increase your distress tolerance. How does that work? Start at the very basic level: I’m going to make eye contact with somebody for one second and then look away. Great, boom, done. That’s the first level on the flirting ladder. Next level, I’m going to hold it for three seconds. It’s in small steps. Plan to do it in small, bite-sized steps so that you can increase your distress tolerance window. What flirting can be is a practice that you build up gradually towards. So wherever you are on the flirting ladder, if you’ve never made eye contact with somebody, you’re super shy, you’ve never gone up to a cute stranger and said hello, just literally write down five simple steps that you could do this week: eye contact, saying hello. One of my clients did a wink and run. When you plan to do something courageous and say, “I’m going to do it for 10 seconds and then I can bail,” you’re more likely to do courageous things. You’re more likely to have more connections in your life and you’re more likely to meet the right people for you.
